title: Grade 3 daily reading
overview: One hundred eighty nights of authentic public-domain poetry, stories, myth, nature writing, and devotional prose, read together and gradually more independently. The year opens with short complete poems by Blake and Montgomery, Anna Botsford Comstock’s historical nature observations, Barbauld’s prose hymns, and two-night Just So Stories. It then lengthens into connected runs: Roberts’s realistic animal stories, Nesbit’s comic dragon tales, Ingelow’s fairy journey, the second half of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, the first six chapters of Through the Looking-Glass, Hawthorne’s retellings of Midas and Pandora, and two serial installments of Little Lord Fauntleroy. A week of poems and observation separates each longer run. Long scenes stay contiguous and carry recaps; adults read the longest passages aloud, while selected short poems, observations, and late-year serial scenes invite an independent first reading. The 15–20 minute estimates include rereading and discussion; they are teaching judgments, not speed targets. Historical views on religion, rank, gender, and nature are named as features of their authors and times.

progression.focus: Listen and reread for sound, sequence, and precise observation.
progression.rationale: Short complete poems, single nature-study observations, two Barbauld hymns, and two-night Just So Stories keep each night small enough to reread. Children locate words that answer a question before explaining what they show.

progression.focus: Follow animal stories to their endings and separate observation from the narrator’s interpretation.
progression.rationale: Three Roberts animal stories, each read to its own ending over consecutive nights, lengthen passages to roughly 500–1,000 words and build on the observation habits from Comstock. Readers ask what a storyteller adds to tracks, sounds and movements, and how each story’s ending, including the deaths that define the genre, changes the meaning of what came before. Week 10 returns to poems and observation.

progression.focus: Track a problem and its solution through a whole comic tale.
progression.rationale: Nesbit’s Book of Dragons supplies the year’s first long tales, mostly over consecutive nights; adults read the longest scenes aloud. Questions ask children to reconstruct plans, reversals, and the narrator’s jokes, and to tell an expectation from an outcome. Week 15 is a change-of-pace week that includes an independent poem.

progression.focus: Infer the rules of an invented world from scattered details.
progression.rationale: Selected scenes from Mopsa the Fairy require holding earlier situations in memory with the help of recaps, and explaining why a fantasy place behaves as it does. Week 19 returns to poetry and observation.

progression.focus: Distinguish speakers and test arguments in dialogue, nonsense, and parody.
progression.rationale: Alice chapters VII–XII run continuously from the tea party to the trial. Children follow quick dialogue, notice when a character’s logic fails, and read parody verse aloud. Week 24 offers short independent observations.

progression.focus: Use structure and reversal to interpret a dream world and its poems.
progression.rationale: Through the Looking-Glass chapters I–VI ask readers to explain mirror-reversals, compare characters’ interpretations of Jabberwocky and The Walrus and the Carpenter, and support a view of who is dreaming. Week 29 returns to poems and observation.

progression.focus: Weigh a character’s choices and the storyteller’s comments in retold myth.
progression.rationale: Hawthorne’s Golden Touch and Paradise of Children are long, ornate retellings with an intrusive narrator. Discussion asks for more than one piece of evidence and allows different judgments of Midas, Pandora, and Epimetheus. Week 33 brings the last poems and observations.

progression.focus: Read shorter serial scenes first on one’s own, then connect character change to evidence.
progression.rationale: Two 1886 St. Nicholas installments of Little Lord Fauntleroy have shorter scenes, several marked for an independent first reading followed by shared rereading. Questions ask how a community, a grandfather, and a family reunion reveal change over a whole serial chapter. Independent nights are selective, not a claim that every classic suits unaided Grade 3 decoding.

days.title: Introduction (Songs of Innocence)
days.challenge: Follow the changes from piping to singing to writing; reread with three different voices.
days.focus: How a song becomes a book for more children.
days.context: A child on a cloud asks a piper to change how he shares his songs.

excerpt.locator: Introduction (Songs of Innocence); complete work, 5 source blocks; opens “Piping down the valleys wild, Piping songs of pleasant glee, On a …”; closes “… And I wrote my happy songs Every child may joy to hear.”.

blocks.text:
Piping down the valleys wild,
Piping songs of pleasant glee,
On a cloud I saw a child,
And he laughing said to me:

‘Pipe a song about a Lamb!’
So I piped with merry cheer.
‘Piper, pipe that song again.’
So I piped: he wept to hear.

‘Drop thy pipe, thy happy pipe;
Sing thy songs of happy cheer!’
So I sung the same again,
While he wept with joy to hear.

‘Piper, sit thee down and write
In a book, that all may read.’
So he vanished from my sight;
And I plucked a hollow reed,

And I made a rural pen,
And I stained the water clear,
And I wrote my happy songs
Every child may joy to hear.

questions.prompt: What does the child ask for after hearing the pipe?
facilitatorNotes: First the child asks for the pipe song again, then a sung version, then a written book; trace the requests in order.
evidence: Sing thy songs of happy cheer!

questions.prompt: Are the child’s tears evidence that the song is sad?
facilitatorNotes: No: the speaker explicitly says they are tears of joy. A happy work can move a listener deeply.
evidence: While he wept with joy to hear.

questions.prompt: Why does writing change who can enjoy the songs?
facilitatorNotes: The child on the cloud disappears, but a book can reach every child, including readers beyond the valley.
evidence: In a book, that all may read.

days.title: Morning Along Shore
days.challenge: Use a second reading to distinguish actual sea sights from imaginary voices.
days.focus: The sea as an invitation to wake and notice.
days.context: Read the whole poem aloud, then reread the lines that make the shore seem alive.

excerpt.locator: Morning Along Shore; complete work, 6 source blocks; opens “Hark, oh hark the elfin laughter All the little waves along, As …”; closes “… for antic wind and billow When the morn is on the wave!”.

blocks.text:
Hark, oh hark the elfin laughter
All the little waves along,
As if echoes speeding after
Mocked a merry merman's song!

All the gulls are out, delighting
In a wild, uncharted quest—
See the first red sunshine smiting
Silver sheen of wing and breast!

Ho, the sunrise rainbow-hearted
Steals athwart the misty brine,
And the sky where clouds have parted
Is a bowl of amber wine!

Sweet, its cradle-lilt partaking,
Dreams that hover o'er the sea,
But the lyric of its waking
Is a sweeter thing to me!

Who would drowze in dull devotion
To his ease when dark is done,
And upon its breast the ocean
Like a jewel wears the sun?

"Up, forsake a lazy pillow!"
Calls the sea from cleft and cave,
Ho, for antic wind and billow
When the morn is on the wave!

questions.prompt: Which two colors appear on the gulls as the sun rises?
facilitatorNotes: Red sunshine strikes the silver wings and breasts; the colors come from light and feathers.
evidence:
See the first red sunshine smiting
Silver sheen of wing and breast!

questions.prompt: What comparison makes the ocean seem to wear the sun?
facilitatorNotes: The sun is a jewel on the ocean’s breast; the reflected brightness suggests decoration.
evidence: Like a jewel wears the sun?

questions.prompt: Why does the poem end with a command about a pillow?
facilitatorNotes: The lively shore calls the sleeper outdoors; the command completes the speaker’s preference for waking over dreams.
evidence: Up, forsake a lazy pillow!

days.title: The Shepherd
days.challenge: Pause at line endings without breaking each sentence; explain “nigh” from context.
days.focus: Watchfulness within a peaceful scene.
days.context: A shepherd speaks no dialogue here: the poem describes his work and the sounds he hears.

excerpt.locator: The Shepherd; complete work, 2 source blocks; opens “How sweet is the shepherd’s sweet lot! From the morn to the …”; closes “… they are in peace, For they know when their shepherd is nigh.”.

blocks.text:
How sweet is the shepherd’s sweet lot!
From the morn to the evening he strays;
He shall follow his sheep all the day,
And his tongue shall be fillèd with praise.

For he hears the lambs’ innocent call,
And he hears the ewes’ tender reply;
He is watchful while they are in peace,
For they know when their shepherd is nigh.

questions.prompt: Does the shepherd leave after checking the flock once?
facilitatorNotes: No, the description extends from morning to evening and all day.
evidence: He shall follow his sheep all the day,

questions.prompt: Which two sheep voices does he hear?
facilitatorNotes: The lambs call and the ewes, or adult female sheep, reply; the paired voices create a family scene.
evidence: And he hears the ewes’ tender reply;

questions.prompt: Why can watchfulness and peace belong in the same scene?
facilitatorNotes: The sheep can be peaceful because their shepherd remains near and attentive; peaceful does not mean unattended.
evidence: He is watchful while they are in peace,

days.title: The Chipmunk — an acorn-gathering observation (excerpt)
days.challenge: Slow down a long paragraph and separate the observer’s first guess from her correction.
days.focus: Evidence that changes an identification.
days.context: Comstock watches an animal outside her window. Sketch its sequence of actions after rereading.

excerpt.locator: The Chipmunk — an acorn-gathering observation (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 1 source blocks; opens “WHILE the chipmunk is a good runner and jumper, it is not …”; closes “… discovered, although it was well hidden by a bunch of orchard grass.”.

blocks.text: WHILE the chipmunk is a good runner and jumper, it is not so able a climber as is the red squirrel, and it naturally stays nearer the ground. One windy day I was struck by the peculiar attitude of what, I first thought, was a red squirrel gathering green acorns from a chestnut oak in front of my window. A second glance showed me that it was a chipmunk lying close to the branch, hanging on for “dear life” and with an attitude of extreme caution, quite foreign to the red squirrel in a similar situation. It would creep out, seize an acorn in its teeth, creep back to a larger limb, take off the shell, and with its little paws stuff the kernel into its cheek pouches; it took hold of one side of its mouth with one hand to stretch it out, as if opening a bag, and stuffed the acorn in with the other. I do not know whether this process was necessary or not at the beginning, for his cheeks were distended when I first saw him; and he kept on stuffing them until he looked as if he had a hopeless case of mumps. Then with obvious care he descended the tree and retreated to his den in the side hill, the door of which I had already discovered, although it was well hidden by a bunch of orchard grass.

questions.prompt: What did Comstock first think she was watching? What changed her mind?
facilitatorNotes: She first thought red squirrel, then noticed a chipmunk lying close to the branch with unusual caution.
evidence: A second glance showed me that it was a chipmunk

questions.prompt: How did the animal move an acorn from the tree toward its den?
facilitatorNotes: It took the acorn in its teeth, returned to a larger branch, shelled it, and packed the kernel in its cheek pouch before descending.
evidence: take off the shell, and with its little paws stuff the kernel into its cheek pouches;

questions.prompt: Where does Comstock admit a limit to her observation?
facilitatorNotes: She did not see the beginning, so she cannot know whether using a paw to stretch the cheek was necessary then.
evidence: I do not know whether this process was necessary or not at the beginning

days.title: The Echoing Green
days.challenge: Track morning play, remembered play, and evening rest across three stanzas.
days.focus: A public green connecting children and older people.
days.context: A green is an open grassy place where people gather. Read the repeated final words carefully.

excerpt.locator: The Echoing Green; complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “The sun does arise, And make happy the skies; The merry bells …”; closes “… ready for rest, And sport no more seen On the darkening green.”.

blocks.text:
Old John, with white hair,
Does laugh away care,
Sitting under the oak,
Among the old folk.
They laugh at our play,
And soon they all say,
‘Such, such were the joys
When we all—girls and boys—
In our youth-time were seen
On the echoing green.’

Till the little ones, weary,
No more can be merry:
The sun does descend,
And our sports have an end.
Round the laps of their mothers
Many sisters and brothers,
Like birds in their nest,
Are ready for rest,
And sport no more seen
On the darkening green.

questions.prompt: What makes the first stanza noisy and cheerful?
facilitatorNotes: Bells and several birds sing around the children’s sports; accept a precise pair of sounds.
evidence:
The birds of the bush,
Sing louder around

questions.prompt: Why do the older people enjoy watching the children?
facilitatorNotes: The play reminds them of their own childhood joys.
evidence:
Such, such were the joys
When we all—girls and boys—

questions.prompt: How does the final description of the green differ from the earlier refrain?
facilitatorNotes: Echoing becomes darkening as play ends; this follows sunset and the children’s tiredness.
evidence: On the darkening green.

days.title: Come, Rest Awhile
days.challenge: Read the short couplets twice, following the invitation across stanza boundaries.
days.focus: What hurried people fail to notice.
days.context: The speaker invites a busy listener to step away from a marketplace and street. “Mart” means market.

excerpt.locator: Come, Rest Awhile; complete work, 8 source blocks; opens “Come, rest awhile, and let us idly stray In glimmering valleys, cool …”; closes “… what it is to smile In your too busy life—come, rest awhile.”.

blocks.text:
Come, rest awhile, and let us idly stray
In glimmering valleys, cool and far away.

Come from the greedy mart, the troubled street,
And listen to the music, faint and sweet,

That echoes ever to a listening ear,
Unheard by those who will not pause to hear—

The wayward chimes of memory's pensive bells,
Wind-blown o'er misty hills and curtained dells.

One step aside and dewy buds unclose
The sweetness of the violet and the rose;

Song and romance still linger in the green,
Emblossomed ways by you so seldom seen,

And near at hand, would you but see them, lie
All lovely things beloved in days gone by.

You have forgotten what it is to smile
In your too busy life—come, rest awhile.

questions.prompt: What places does the listener leave, and what place replaces them?
facilitatorNotes: The troubled street and greedy market give way to cool glimmering valleys; the contrast suggests relief.
evidence: Come from the greedy mart, the troubled street,

questions.prompt: According to the poem, why is some music unheard?
facilitatorNotes: People who refuse to pause miss it; the poem makes attention a choice.
evidence: Unheard by those who will not pause to hear—

questions.prompt: Does the listener need a distant journey to find lovely things?
facilitatorNotes: Not necessarily: the poem says one step aside and near at hand, suggesting nearby overlooked beauty.
evidence: And near at hand, would you but see them, lie

days.title: Laughing Song
days.challenge: Give the repeated “laugh” different shades of sound without rushing.
days.focus: An invitation that lets landscape join a human celebration.
days.context: The whole poem imagines a countryside picnic as a shared laugh.

excerpt.locator: Laughing Song; complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “When the green woods laugh with the voice of joy, And the …”; closes “… join with me, To sing the sweet chorus of ‘Ha ha he!’”.

blocks.text:
When the meadows laugh with lively green,
And the grasshopper laughs in the merry scene;
When Mary and Susan and Emily
With their sweet round mouths sing ‘Ha ha he!’

When the painted birds laugh in the shade,
Where our table with cherries and nuts is spread:
Come live, and be merry, and join with me,
To sing the sweet chorus of ‘Ha ha he!’

questions.prompt: Name one thing that cannot literally laugh but laughs in this poem.
facilitatorNotes: Woods, stream, air, hill, meadow, or grasshopper are personified; explain the chosen image rather than treating it as a fact.
evidence: And the dimpling stream runs laughing by;

questions.prompt: What small detail tells us people have prepared food together?
facilitatorNotes: A table has cherries and nuts spread on it; it helps the cheerful scene feel like a gathering.
evidence: Where our table with cherries and nuts is spread:

questions.prompt: How does the final invitation change our place in the scene?
facilitatorNotes: Readers move from watching others to being asked to join the chorus.
evidence: Come live, and be merry, and join with me,

days.title: A Winter Dawn
days.challenge: Unpack two dense stanzas by drawing the sky before and after dawn.
days.focus: Light described as a contest with shadow.
days.context: “Orient” means the east; “marge” means edge. Reread the colors after a first shared reading.

excerpt.locator: A Winter Dawn; complete work, 2 source blocks; opens “Above the marge of night a star still shines, And on the …”; closes “… in twain the gray Banners of shadow hosts, and lo, the day!”.

blocks.text:
Above the marge of night a star still shines,
And on the frosty hills the sombre pines
Harbor an eerie wind that crooneth low
Over the glimmering wastes of virgin snow.

Through the pale arch of orient the morn
Comes in a milk-white splendor newly-born,
A sword of crimson cuts in twain the gray
Banners of shadow hosts, and lo, the day!

questions.prompt: What remains visible before dawn?
facilitatorNotes: A star still shines over the night’s edge; pines and snow are also visible in the dimness.
evidence: Above the marge of night a star still shines,

questions.prompt: How does the poem move from quiet to forceful action?
facilitatorNotes: It begins with a low crooning wind, then uses a sword cutting banners for the sudden bright dawn.
evidence: A sword of crimson cuts in twain the gray

questions.prompt: Is the sword a literal weapon? What sight might it describe?
facilitatorNotes: It is an image for a red beam or band of sunrise cutting across gray darkness; accept other grounded visual explanations.
evidence: Banners of shadow hosts, and lo, the day!

days.title: Hymn I
days.challenge: Follow repeated “He” and “I” to identify who acts in each sentence.
days.focus: A child speaker gaining a voice.
days.context: This is a complete prose hymn: it does not need rhyme to use repetition and rhythm. Read it as a historical author’s viewpoint.
days.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian devotional text speaks from its author’s faith. Its claims about God are beliefs, not beliefs readers must adopt; older forms such as “hath” mean “has.”

excerpt.locator: Hymn I; complete work, 11 source blocks; opens “COME, let us praise God, for he is exceeding great; let us …”; closes “… will never forget God, so long as my life remaineth in me.”.

blocks.text: COME, let us praise God, for he is exceeding great; let us bless God, for he is very good.
He made all things; the sun to rule the day, the moon to shine by night.
He made the great whale, and the elephant; and the little worm that crawleth on the ground.
The little birds sing praises to God, when they warble sweetly in the green shade.
The brooks and rivers praise God, when they murmur melodiously amongst the smooth pebbles.
I will praise God with my voice; for I may praise him, though I am but a little child.
A few years ago, and I was a little infant, and my tongue was dumb within my mouth:
And I did not know the great name of God, for my reason was not come unto me.
But now I can speak, and my tongue shall praise him; I can think of all his kindness, and my heart shall love him.
Let him call me, and I will come unto him; let him command, and I will obey him.
When I am older, I will praise him better; and I will never forget God, so long as my life remaineth in me.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention both an elephant and a little worm?
facilitatorNotes: The size contrast extends the claim of creation to large and small living things.
evidence: the elephant; and the little worm

questions.prompt: What ability does the speaker have now that the infant lacked?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker can speak and think about kindness; “dumb” here means unable to speak, not unintelligent.
evidence: But now I can speak, and my tongue shall praise him;

questions.prompt: Why is the ending about being older rather than about today alone?
facilitatorNotes: The child expects praise and understanding to grow and promises continuing remembrance.
evidence: When I am older, I will praise him better;

days.title: The Chipmunk — the bonnet mystery (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish a witnessed result from an unsolved explanation.
days.focus: An observational anecdote with a comic ending.
days.context: A naturalist’s tame chipmunk hides walnuts. This is a historical pet anecdote; observe wild animals at a respectful distance today.

excerpt.locator: The Chipmunk — the bonnet mystery (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 1 source blocks; opens “Chipmunks are more easily tamed than red squirrels and soon learn that …”; closes “… get into the bonnet-box, the cover of which was always carefully closed.”.

blocks.text: Chipmunks are more easily tamed than red squirrels and soon learn that pockets may contain nuts and other things good to eat. The first tame chipmunk of my acquaintance belonged to a species found in the California mountains. He was a beautiful little creature and loved to play about his mistress’ room; she being a naturalist as well as a poet, was able to understand her little companion, and the relations between them were full of mutual confidence. He was fond of English walnuts and would always hide away all that were placed in a dish on the table. One day his mistress, when taking off her bonnet after returning from church, discovered several of these nuts tucked safely in the velvet bows; they were invisible from the front but perfectly visible from the side. Even yet, she wonders what the people at church that day thought of her original ideas in millinery; and she wonders still more how “Chipsie” managed to get into the bonnet-box, the cover of which was always carefully closed.

questions.prompt: What habit prepares us for the surprise in the bonnet?
facilitatorNotes: The chipmunk routinely hides every walnut placed on the table.
evidence: would always hide away all that were placed in a dish on the table.

questions.prompt: Why might people at church see what the wearer did not?
facilitatorNotes: The nuts were hidden from the front but visible from the side.
evidence: they were invisible from the front but perfectly visible from the side.

questions.prompt: What question remains unanswered at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The writer does not know how Chipsie entered the closed bonnet-box; the anecdote preserves the mystery instead of inventing an explanation.
evidence: the cover of which was always carefully closed.

days.title: Nurse’s Song (Songs of Innocence)
days.challenge: Use separate voices for the nurse and the children, and identify the compromise.
days.focus: An argument that ends in trust and more play.
days.context: A nurse here is an adult caring for children. The children answer her request to come home.

excerpt.locator: Nurse’s Song (Songs of Innocence); complete work, 4 source blocks; opens “When voices of children are heard on the green, And laughing is …”; closes “… little ones leaped, and shouted, and laughed, And all the hills echoèd.”.

blocks.text:
When voices of children are heard on the green,
And laughing is heard on the hill,
My heart is at rest within my breast,
And everything else is still.

‘Then come home, my children, the sun is gone down,
And the dews of night arise;
Come, come, leave off play, and let us away,
Till the morning appears in the skies.’

‘No, no, let us play, for it is yet day,
And we cannot go to sleep;
Besides, in the sky the little birds fly,
And the hills are all covered with sheep.’

‘Well, well, go and play till the light fades away,
And then go home to bed.’
The little ones leaped, and shouted, and laughed,
And all the hills echoèd.

questions.prompt: What makes the nurse think it is time to stop playing?
facilitatorNotes: The sun has gone down and night dew is rising.
evidence:
the sun is gone down,
And the dews of night arise;

questions.prompt: What outdoor evidence do the children offer in reply?
facilitatorNotes: They point to flying birds and sheep still on the hills to argue that usable daylight remains.
evidence: in the sky the little birds fly,

questions.prompt: Does the nurse give permission without a limit?
facilitatorNotes: No: she allows play until the light fades, then they must go to bed.
evidence: go and play till the light fades away,

days.title: For Little Things
days.challenge: Connect four small sensory moments with the final statement of thanks.
days.focus: Why ordinary sights can carry great value.
days.context: The speaker remembers night and morning before naming what matters. Read the last stanza after recalling the earlier images.
days.contentNote: This poem expresses the author’s Christian belief. Discuss that viewpoint without asking readers to share it.

excerpt.locator: For Little Things; complete work, 5 source blocks; opens “Last night I looked across the hills And through an arch of …”; closes “… But most I thank Thee humbly for The joy of little things.”.

blocks.text:
Last night I looked across the hills
And through an arch of darkling pine
Low-swung against a limpid west
I saw a young moon shine.

And as I gazed there blew a wind,
Loosed where the sylvan shadows stir,
Bringing delight to soul and sense
The breath of dying fir.

This morn I saw a dancing host
Of poppies in a garden way,
And straight my heart was mirth-possessed
And I was glad as they.

I heard a song across the sea
As sweet and faint as echoes are,
And glimpsed a poignant happiness
No care of earth might mar.

Dear God, our life is beautiful
In every splendid gift it brings,
But most I thank Thee humbly for
The joy of little things.

questions.prompt: What natural shape frames the young moon?
facilitatorNotes: An arch of dark pines frames it, making a small view seem carefully set apart.
evidence: through an arch of darkling pine

questions.prompt: Which garden sight changes the speaker’s mood?
facilitatorNotes: The dancing poppies make the speaker feel glad, as though sharing their happiness.
evidence: And straight my heart was mirth-possessed

questions.prompt: Why is “most” important in the final stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker appreciates splendid gifts but gives greatest thanks for little joys; this explains the small-scale examples.
evidence:
But most I thank Thee humbly for
The joy of little things.

days.title: The Blossom
days.challenge: Compare two almost parallel stanzas and notice the altered emotion.
days.focus: One shelter holding joy and sorrow.
days.context: The poem lets a blossom see and hear birds. “Bosom” suggests a close, sheltered place.

excerpt.locator: The Blossom; complete work, 2 source blocks; opens “Merry, merry sparrow! Under leaves so green A happy blossom Sees you, …”; closes “… happy blossom Hears you sobbing, sobbing, Pretty, pretty robin, Near my bosom.”.

blocks.text:
Merry, merry sparrow!
Under leaves so green
A happy blossom
Sees you, swift as arrow,
Seek your cradle narrow,
Near my bosom.

Pretty, pretty robin!
Under leaves so green
A happy blossom
Hears you sobbing, sobbing,
Pretty, pretty robin,
Near my bosom.

questions.prompt: Which bird moves swiftly in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The sparrow is compared to an arrow; the quick motion contrasts with the safe cradle it seeks.
evidence: Sees you, swift as arrow,

questions.prompt: What changes when the robin appears?
facilitatorNotes: The blossom hears sobbing instead of simply seeing swift movement; the emotion becomes sorrowful.
evidence: Hears you sobbing, sobbing,

questions.prompt: What stays the same for both birds?
facilitatorNotes: Both remain near the blossom’s bosom beneath green leaves; the repeated shelter includes different feelings.
evidence: Under leaves so green

days.title: On the Bay
days.challenge: Keep track of departure and return through two changing skies.
days.focus: Work, danger, and welcome in a circular journey.
days.context: The poem follows one fisherman’s imagined day. A harbor bar is a shallow ridge near its entrance.
days.contentNote: The poem briefly mentions the dangers of fishing and uses prayer as part of its character’s home life.

excerpt.locator: On the Bay; complete work, 4 source blocks; opens “When the salt wave laps on the long, dim shore, And frets …”; closes “… reef is dim And a true heart is waiting to welcome him!”.

blocks.text:
When the salt wave laps on the long, dim shore,
And frets the reef with its windy sallies,
And the dawn's white light is threading once more
The purple firs in the landward valleys,
While yet the arms of the wide gray sea
Are cradling the sunrise that is to be,
The fisherman's boat, through the mist afar,
Has sailed in the wake of the morning star.

The wind in his cordage and canvas sings
Its old glad song of strength and endeavor,
And up from the heart of the ocean rings
A call of courage and cheer forever;
Toil and danger and stress may wait
Beyond the arch of the morning's gate,
But he knows that behind him, upon the shore,
A true heart prays for him evermore.

When a young moon floats in the hollow sky,
Like a fairy shallop, all pale and golden,
And over the rocks that are grim and high,
The lamp of the light-house aloft is holden;
When the bay is like to a lucent cup
With glamor and glory and glow filled up,
In the track of the sunset, across the foam,
The fisherman's boat comes sailing home.

The wind is singing a low, sweet song
Of a rest well won and a toil well over,
And there on the shore shines clear and strong
The star of the homelight to guide the rover:
And deep unto deep may call and wail
But the fisherman laughs as he furls his sail,
For the bar is passed and the reef is dim
And a true heart is waiting to welcome him!

questions.prompt: Which light accompanies the departure?
facilitatorNotes: The morning star appears as dawn threads the trees; the sunrise has not fully arrived.
evidence: Has sailed in the wake of the morning star.

questions.prompt: How does the later wind-song differ from the earlier one?
facilitatorNotes: First it sings strength and effort; later it sings rest after completed work.
evidence: Of a rest well won and a toil well over,

questions.prompt: Why does the fisherman laugh even though the deep still wails?
facilitatorNotes: He has crossed the dangerous bar and is welcomed by someone on shore; his local safety contrasts with the sea beyond.
evidence: For the bar is passed and the reef is dim

days.title: The Dandelion — whose garden? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate precise measurement from the writer’s pretend conversation with a plant.
days.focus: Admiration complicating a gardener’s annoyance.
days.context: Read the two paragraphs as a historical observer’s lively account; “rosette” describes leaves spreading around a center.

excerpt.locator: The Dandelion — whose garden? (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 2 source blocks; opens “It is very difficult for us, when we watch the behavior of …”; closes “… to eat them, and thus the plants are safe even in pastures.”.

blocks.text: It is very difficult for us, when we watch the behavior of the dandelions, not to attribute to them thinking power, they have so many ways of getting ahead of us. I always look at a dandelion and talk to it as if it were a real person. One spring when all the vegetables in my garden were callow weaklings, I found there, in their midst, a dandelion rosette with ten great leaves spreading out and completely shading a circle ten inches in diameter; I said, “Look here, Madam, this is my garden!” and I pulled up the squatter. But I could not help paying admiring tribute to the taproot, which lacked only an inch of being a foot in length. It was smooth, whitish, fleshy and, when cut, bled a milky juice showing that it was full of food; and it was as strong from the end-pull as a whipcord; it also had a bunch of rather fine rootlets about an inch below the surface of the soil and an occasional rootlet farther down; and then I said “Madam, I beg your pardon; I think this was your garden and not mine.”

Dandelion leaves afford an excellent study in variation of form. The edges of the leaf are notched in a peculiar way, so that the lobes were, by some one, supposed to look like lions’ teeth in profile; thus the plant was called in France “dents-de-lion” (teeth of the lion), and we have made from this the name dandelion. The leaves are so bitter that grazing animals do not like to eat them, and thus the plants are safe even in pastures.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock first object to the dandelion?
facilitatorNotes: Its broad leaves shade her small vegetables and occupy her garden space.
evidence: completely shading a circle ten inches in diameter;

questions.prompt: What causes her playful apology?
facilitatorNotes: She admires the long, strong, food-filled taproot and imagines the well-established plant as the garden’s rightful owner.
evidence: I think this was your garden and not mine.

questions.prompt: How do the leaves help explain the name dandelion?
facilitatorNotes: Their pointed lobes suggested lions’ teeth; the French name is explained in the second paragraph.
evidence: dents-de-lion

days.title: Spring (Songs of Innocence)
days.challenge: Hold a steady rhythm through short lines and a long repeated refrain.
days.focus: Children, birds, and a lamb joining a seasonal welcome.
days.context: Read each stanza once, then join in the recurring final line.

excerpt.locator: Spring (Songs of Innocence); complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “Sound the flute! Now it’s mute! Birds delight, Day and night, Nightingale, …”; closes “… me kiss Your soft face; Merrily, merrily we welcome in the year.”.

blocks.text:
Sound the flute!
Now it’s mute!
Birds delight,
Day and night,
Nightingale,
In the dale,
Lark in sky,—
Merrily,
Merrily, merrily to welcome in the year.

questions.prompt: What sound begins the poem, and what happens immediately afterward?
facilitatorNotes: A flute sounds and then becomes mute; bird voices take over the lively scene.
evidence:
Sound the flute!
Now it’s mute!

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza connect children with the birds?
facilitatorNotes: The crowing cock is followed by “So do you”; children’s cheerful noise joins the birds’ calls.
evidence:
Cock does crow,
So do you;

questions.prompt: What changes in the last refrain?
facilitatorNotes: “To welcome” becomes “we welcome”: the speaker now includes everyone in an active shared greeting.
evidence: Merrily, merrily we welcome in the year.

days.title: Rain on the Hill
days.challenge: Trace a sound pattern from stillness through wind to many moods.
days.focus: Weather imagined as a companion.
days.context: The poem moves through three stages. “Balsam” is a tree scent and “dole” means sorrow.

excerpt.locator: Rain on the Hill; complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “Now on the hill The fitful wind is so still That never …”; closes “… rain we find Fellowship meet for each change of mood or mind.”.

blocks.text:
Now on the hill
The fitful wind is so still
That never a wimpling mist uplifts,
Nor a trembling leaf drop-laden stirs;
From the ancient firs
Aroma of balsam drifts,
And the silent places are filled
With elusive odors distilled
By the rain from asters empearled and frilled,
And a wild wet savor that dwells
Far adown in tawny fallows and bracken dells.

Then with a rush,
Breaking the beautiful hush
Where the only sound was the lisping, low
Converse of raindrops, or the dear sound
Close to the ground,
That grasses make when they grow,
Comes the wind in a gay,
Rollicking, turbulent way,
To winnow each bough and toss each spray,
Piping and whistling in glee
With the vibrant notes of a merry minstrelsy.

The friendly rain
Sings many a haunting strain,
Now of gladness and now of dole,
Anon of the glamor and the dream
That ever seem
To wait on a pilgrim soul;
Yea, we can hear
The grief of an elder year,
And laughter half-forgotten and dear;
In the wind and the rain we find
Fellowship meet for each change of mood or mind.

questions.prompt: Which sense is especially important before the wind arrives?
facilitatorNotes: Smell: balsam and wet plants fill the still places with odors.
evidence: Aroma of balsam drifts,

questions.prompt: Which words make the wind’s arrival feel sudden?
facilitatorNotes: “Then with a rush” and “Breaking” interrupt the hush; the later piping and whistling add movement and sound.
evidence:
Then with a rush,
Breaking the beautiful hush

questions.prompt: Is the rain’s song always happy?
facilitatorNotes: No; it carries gladness, sorrow, remembered grief, and laughter, making room for changing feelings.
evidence: Now of gladness and now of dole,

days.title: Hymn III
days.challenge: Follow three repeated patterns: caretaker, question, and religious answer.
days.focus: An argument built from familiar relationships.
days.context: The author compares God with a shepherd, a parent, and a king. These are the author’s beliefs and historical images of authority.
days.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian devotional text speaks from its author’s faith. Its claims about God are beliefs, not beliefs readers must adopt; older forms such as “hath” mean “has.”

excerpt.locator: Hymn III; complete work, 10 source blocks; opens “Behold the Shepherd of the flock, he taketh care for his sheep, …”; closes “… will love him: God is our King, therefore we will obey him.”.

blocks.text: Behold the Shepherd of the flock, he taketh care for his sheep, he leadeth them among clear brooks, he guideth them to fresh pasture; if the young lambs are weary, he carrieth them in his arms; if they wander, he bringeth them back.
But who is the shepherd's shepherd? who taketh care for him? who guideth him in the path he should go? and if he wander, who shall bring him back?

God is the shepherd's shepherd. He is the Shepherd over all; he taketh care for all; the whole earth is his fold: we are all his flock; and every herb, and every green field is the pasture which he hath prepared for us.

The mother loveth her little child; she bringeth it up on her knees; she nourisheth its body with food; she feedeth its mind with knowledge: if it is sick, she nurseth it with tender love; she watcheth over it when asleep; she forgetteth it not for a moment; she teacheth it how to be good; she rejoiceth daily in its growth.

But who is the parent of the mother? who nourisheth her with good things, and watcheth over her with ten- der love, and remembereth her every moment? Whose arms are about her to guard her from harm? and if she is sick, who shall heal her?
God is the parent of the mother; he is the parent of all, for he created all. All the men, and all the women who are alive in the wide world, are his children; he loveth all, he is good to all.

The king governeth his people; he hath a golden crown upon his head, and the royal sceptre is in his hand; he sitteth upon a throne, and sendeth forth his commands; his subjects fear before him; if they do well, he protecteth them from danger; and if they do evil, he punisheth them.
But who is the sovereign of the king? who commandeth him what he must do? whose hand is stretched out to protect him from danger? and if he doeth evil, who shall punish him?

God is the sovereign of the king; his crown is of rays of light, and his throne is amongst the stars. He is King of kings, and Lord of lords: if he biddeth us live, we live; and if he biddeth us die, we die: his dominion is over all worlds, and the light of his countenance is upon all his works.
God is our Shepherd, therefore we will follow him: God is our Father, therefore we will love him: God is our King, therefore we will obey him.

questions.prompt: What does the shepherd do when a lamb is too tired to walk?
facilitatorNotes: He carries it; this concrete act begins the larger comparison about care.
evidence: if the young lambs are weary, he carrieth them in his arms;

questions.prompt: How does the paragraph about a mother distinguish feeding body and mind?
facilitatorNotes: Food nourishes the body, while knowledge feeds the mind; both count as care in the comparison.
evidence: she feedeth its mind with knowledge:

questions.prompt: Which three responses does the ending connect with its three images of God?
facilitatorNotes: Following corresponds to shepherd, loving to father, and obeying to king; discuss how the repeated structure builds the author’s argument.
evidence: God is our Shepherd, therefore we will follow him:

days.title: Infant Joy
days.challenge: Infer speakers when quotation marks do not name them.
days.focus: Naming through imagined conversation and song.
days.context: An adult imagines a newborn who can speak. Read this very short poem several times, trying possible voices.

excerpt.locator: Infant Joy; complete work, 2 source blocks; opens “‘I have no name; I am but two days old.’ What shall …”; closes “… thee: Thou dost smile, I sing the while; Sweet joy befall thee!”.

blocks.text:
‘I have no name;
I am but two days old.’
What shall I call thee?
‘I happy am,
Joy is my name.’
Sweet joy befall thee!

Pretty joy!
Sweet joy, but two days old.
Sweet joy I call thee:
Thou dost smile,
I sing the while;
Sweet joy befall thee!

questions.prompt: What tells us the infant has only just been born?
facilitatorNotes: The imagined child says it is two days old and has no name.
evidence: I am but two days old.

questions.prompt: Why is Joy an appropriate name within this conversation?
facilitatorNotes: The infant says it is happy, and the adult notices its smile; the name grows from the exchange.
evidence: I happy am,

questions.prompt: What does the adult do while the baby smiles?
facilitatorNotes: The adult sings and wishes joy for the infant; the ending sounds like a blessing or lullaby.
evidence:
Thou dost smile,
I sing the while;

days.title: An Autumn Evening
days.challenge: Follow one color image through long sentences, then explain a final comparison.
days.focus: Quiet attention filling the observer with delight.
days.context: Crocus can name a flower color; a rune is an old mysterious saying. Read slowly enough to picture the sky.

excerpt.locator: An Autumn Evening; complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “Dark hills against a hollow crocus sky Scarfed with its crimson pennons, …”; closes “… filled, as some deep cup, That with divine enchantment is brimmed up.”.

blocks.text:
Dark hills against a hollow crocus sky
Scarfed with its crimson pennons, and below
The dome of sunset long, hushed valleys lie
Cradling the twilight, where the lone winds blow
And wake among the harps of leafless trees
Fantastic runes and mournful melodies.

The chilly purple air is threaded through
With silver from the rising moon afar,
And from a gulf of clear, unfathomed blue
In the southwest glimmers a great gold star
Above the darkening druid glens of fir
Where beckoning boughs and elfin voices stir.

And so I wander through the shadows still,
And look and listen with a rapt delight,
Pausing again and yet again at will
To drink the elusive beauty of the night,
Until my soul is filled, as some deep cup,
That with divine enchantment is brimmed up.

questions.prompt: What musical instrument do the leafless trees resemble?
facilitatorNotes: Harps: wind passing through them supplies imaginary melodies.
evidence: the harps of leafless trees

questions.prompt: Does the wanderer hurry toward a destination?
facilitatorNotes: No; repeated pauses and looking and listening make the experience itself the purpose.
evidence: Pausing again and yet again at will

questions.prompt: Why compare the soul to a deep cup?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker feels filled by beauty, just as a cup fills with liquid. Different descriptions of the feeling are defensible if grounded in the ending.
evidence: Until my soul is filled, as some deep cup,

days.title: How the Whale Got His Throat — the meal proposed (part 1)
days.challenge: Track who suggests the plan and notice the narrator’s repeated reminder.
days.focus: A small character steering a powerful one.
days.context: In this fanciful origin tale, a hungry Whale talks with a very small fish.
days.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. Kipling’s colonial-era narrator uses exaggerated voices and cultural references; these belong to the historical story.

excerpt.locator: How the Whale Got His Throat — the meal proposed (part 1); contiguous excerpt, 7 source blocks; opens “IN the sea, once upon a time, O my Best Beloved, there …”; closes “… he smacked his lips—so, and turned round three times on his tail.”.

blocks.text: IN the sea, once upon a time, O my Best Beloved, there was a Whale, and he ate fishes. He ate the starfish and the garfish, and the crab and the dab, and the plaice and the dace, and the skate and his mate, and the mackereel and the pickereel, and the really truly twirly-whirly eel. All the fishes he could find in all the sea he ate with his mouth—so! Till at last there was only one small fish left in all the sea, and he was a small 'Stute Fish, and he swam a little behind the Whale's right ear, so as to be out of harm's way. Then the Whale stood up on his tail and said, 'I'm hungry.' And the small 'Stute Fish said in a small 'stute voice, 'Noble and generous Cetacean, have you ever tasted Man?'
'No,' said the Whale. 'What is it like?'
'Nice,' said the small 'Stute Fish. 'Nice but nubbly.'
'Then fetch me some,' said the Whale, and he made the sea froth up with his tail.

'One at a time is enough,' said the 'Stute Fish. 'If you swim to latitude Fifty North, longitude Forty West (that is magic), you will find, sitting on a raft, in the middle of the sea, with nothing on but a pair of blue canvas breeches, a pair of suspenders (you must not forget the suspenders, Best Beloved), and a jack-knife, one shipwrecked Mariner, who, it is only fair to tell you, is a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity.'

So the Whale swam and swam to latitude Fifty North, longitude Forty West, as fast as he could swim, and on a raft, in the middle of the sea, with nothing to wear except a pair of blue canvas breeches, a pair of suspenders (you must particularly remember the suspenders, Best Beloved), and a jack-knife, he found one single, solitary shipwrecked Mariner, trailing his toes in the water. (He had his mummy's leave to paddle, or else he would never have done it, because he was a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity.)

Then the Whale opened his mouth back and back and back till it nearly touched his tail, and he swallowed the shipwrecked Mariner, and the raft he was sitting on, and his blue canvas breeches, and the suspenders (which you must not forget), and the jack-knife—He swallowed them all down into his warm, dark, inside cupboards, and then he smacked his lips—so, and turned round three times on his tail.

questions.prompt: Why does the little fish suggest a new food?
facilitatorNotes: The Whale has eaten many sea creatures; the last little fish redirects his appetite toward Man, protecting itself.
evidence: have you ever tasted Man?

questions.prompt: What unusual detail does the fish give about where to find a man?
facilitatorNotes: It supplies precise latitude and longitude, as if offering navigational instructions.
evidence: latitude Fifty North, longitude Forty West

questions.prompt: Why might the narrator repeat the detail about suspenders?
facilitatorNotes: The reminders signal that the clothing may matter later; readers can predict without yet claiming the outcome.
evidence: you must not forget the suspenders

days.title: How the Whale Got His Throat — the grating (part 2)
days.challenge: Read the action list fluently, then untangle the practical trick.
days.focus: A repeated small detail becoming a solution.
days.context: The Whale has swallowed a shipwrecked Mariner, his raft, and his suspenders. Now the Mariner wants to get home.
days.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story. The Mariner’s rhyme “By means of a grating / I have stopped your ating” plays on an Irish pronunciation of “eating”; the next sentence explains that he was “an Hi-ber-ni-an” (an Irishman). The comic swallowing belongs to the tale.

excerpt.locator: How the Whale Got His Throat — the grating (part 2); contiguous excerpt, 12 source blocks; opens “But as soon as the Mariner, who was a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity, …”; closes “… will know (if you haven't guessed) You're 'Fifty North and Forty West!'”.

blocks.text: But as soon as the Mariner, who was a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity, found himself truly inside the Whale's warm, dark, inside cupboards, he stumped and he jumped and he thumped and he bumped, and he pranced and he danced, and he banged and he clanged, and he hit and he bit, and he leaped and he creeped, and he prowled and he howled, and he hopped and he dropped, and he cried and he sighed, and he crawled and he bawled, and he stepped and he lepped, and he danced hornpipes where he shouldn't, and the Whale felt most unhappy indeed. (Have you forgotten the suspenders?)
So he said to the 'Stute Fish, 'This man is very nubbly, and besides he is making me hiccough. What shall I do?'
'Tell him to come out,' said the 'Stute Fish.
So the Whale called down his own throat to the shipwrecked Mariner, 'Come out and behave yourself. I've got the hiccoughs.'
'Nay, nay!' said the Mariner. 'Not so, but far otherwise. Take me to my natal-shore and the white-cliffs-of-Albion, and I'll think about it.' And he began to dance more than ever.
'You had better take him home,' said the 'Stute Fish to the Whale. 'I ought to have warned you that he is a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity.'

So the Whale swam and swam and swam, with both flippers and his tail, as hard as he could for the hiccoughs; and at last he saw the Mariner's natal-shore and the white-cliffs-of-Albion, and he rushed half-way up the beach, and opened his mouth wide and wide and wide, and said, 'Change here for Winchester, Ashuelot, Nashua, Keene, and stations on the Fitchburg Road;' and just as he said 'Fitch' the Mariner walked out of his mouth. But while the Whale had been swimming, the Mariner, who was indeed a person of infinite-resource-and-sagacity, had taken his jack-knife and cut up the raft into a little square grating all running criss-cross, and he had tied it firm with his suspenders (now you know why you were not to forget the suspenders!), and he dragged that grating good and tight into the Whale's throat, and there it stuck! Then he recited the following Sloka, which, as you have not heard it, I will now proceed to relate—

By means of a grating
I have stopped your ating.

For the Mariner he was also an Hi-ber-ni-an. And he stepped out on the shingle, and went home to his mother, who had given him leave to trail his toes in the water; and he married and lived happily ever afterward. So did the Whale. But from that day on, the grating in his throat, which he could neither cough up nor swallow down, prevented him eating anything except very, very small fish; and that is the reason why whales nowadays never eat men or boys or little girls.
The small 'Stute Fish went and hid himself in the mud under the Door-sills of the Equator. He was afraid that the Whale might be angry with him.

The Sailor took the jack-knife home. He was wearing the blue canvas breeches when he walked out on the shingle. The suspenders were left behind, you see, to tie the grating with; and that is the end of that tale.

When the cabin port-holes are dark and green
Because of the seas outside;
When the ship goes wop (with a wiggle between)
And the steward falls into the soup-tureen,
And the trunks begin to slide;
When Nursey lies on the floor in a heap,
And Mummy tells you to let her sleep,
And you aren't waked or washed or dressed,
Why, then you will know (if you haven't guessed)
You're 'Fifty North and Forty West!'

questions.prompt: How does the Mariner first make the Whale want him out?
facilitatorNotes: He creates a noisy, painful disturbance inside the Whale, making the Whale hiccup.
evidence: he thumped and he bumped

questions.prompt: What two materials become a grating?
facilitatorNotes: The raft is cut into wooden bars and tied with suspenders; the repeated clothing detail now pays off.
evidence: tied it firm with his suspenders

questions.prompt: Why is the ending an invented explanation rather than a report about whales?
facilitatorNotes: The story attributes a whale’s eating limits to an impossible lasting man-made grating and gives animals human speech. The rhyme announces the trick; the passage does not show it causing the change.
evidence:
By means of a grating
I have stopped your ating.

days.title: A Dream
days.challenge: Use context to interpret older words while tracking who hears whom.
days.focus: A tiny lost creature receiving practical help.
days.context: “Emmet” means ant, “hie” means hurry, and “wight” means a being. The scene is a dream.

excerpt.locator: A Dream; complete work, 5 source blocks; opens “Once a dream did weave a shade O’er my angel-guarded bed, That …”; closes “… his round: Follow now the beetle’s hum; Little wanderer, hie thee home!’”.

blocks.text:
Once a dream did weave a shade
O’er my angel-guarded bed,
That an emmet lost its way
Where on grass methought I lay.

Troubled, wildered, and forlorn,
Dark, benighted, travel-worn,
Over many a tangled spray,
All heart-broke, I heard her say:

‘O my children! do they cry,
Do they hear their father sigh?
Now they look abroad to see,
Now return and weep for me.’

Pitying, I dropped a tear:
But I saw a glow-worm near,
Who replied, ‘What wailing wight
Calls the watchman of the night?’

‘I am set to light the ground,
While the beetle goes his round:
Follow now the beetle’s hum;
Little wanderer, hie thee home!’

questions.prompt: What worries the lost ant besides finding her own way?
facilitatorNotes: She imagines her children crying and their father sighing, so the worry is for her family too.
evidence: O my children! do they cry,

questions.prompt: How does the glow-worm describe its job?
facilitatorNotes: It is the watchman who lights the ground at night.
evidence: I am set to light the ground,

questions.prompt: Why does the final advice mention sound rather than light alone?
facilitatorNotes: The ant can follow the beetle’s hum while the glow-worm lights the ground; different creatures help in different ways.
evidence: Follow now the beetle’s hum;

days.title: September
days.challenge: Reread one concentrated stanza and turn its harvest metaphor into plain explanation.
days.focus: Autumn gathering the value of earlier days.
days.context: A sheaf is a tied bundle of grain. The poem imagines a month as a harvest of days.

excerpt.locator: September; complete work, 2 source blocks; opens “SEPTEMBER”; closes “… splendor for the flight Of summer blooms and joys— This is September.”.

blocks.text: SEPTEMBER

Lo! a ripe sheaf of many golden days
Gleaned by the year in autumn's harvest ways,
With here and there, blood-tinted as an ember,
Some crimson poppy of a late delight
Atoning in its splendor for the flight
Of summer blooms and joys—
This is September.

questions.prompt: What is gathered into the imagined sheaf?
facilitatorNotes: Golden days, rather than literal stalks alone; the harvest image suggests valued experiences.
evidence: a ripe sheaf of many golden days

questions.prompt: What flower interrupts the gold with a brighter color?
facilitatorNotes: A late crimson poppy, compared with an ember, adds a vivid surviving delight.
evidence: blood-tinted as an ember,

questions.prompt: Does September mean only the loss of summer?
facilitatorNotes: No; the poem acknowledges vanished summer blooms but finds a new delight that partly makes up for them.
evidence:
Atoning in its splendor for the flight
Of summer blooms and joys—

days.title: The Robin — building a nest (excerpt)
days.challenge: Retell a technical sequence while keeping observed and general claims separate.
days.focus: Materials and actions in a construction account.
days.context: Comstock describes nest construction, including one pair she watched herself. Read twice and list the stages in order.

excerpt.locator: The Robin — building a nest (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 1 source blocks; opens “The beginning of a robin’s nest is very interesting; much strong grass, …”; closes “… are usually four eggs laid which are exquisite greenish blue in color.”.

blocks.text: The beginning of a robin’s nest is very interesting; much strong grass, fine straw, leaves and rootlets are brought and placed on a secure support. When enough of this material is collected and arranged, the bird goes to the nearest mud puddle or stream margin and fills its beak with soft mud and going back “peppers” it into the nest material, and after the latter is soaked the bird gets into it and molds it to the body by nestling and turning around and around. In one case which the author watched the mother bird did this part of the building, although the father worked industriously in bringing the other materials. After the nest is molded but not yet hardened, it is lined with fine grass or rootlets. If the season is very dry and there is no soft mud at hand, the robins can build without the aid of this plaster. There are usually four eggs laid which are exquisite greenish blue in color.

questions.prompt: What comes before the mud is added?
facilitatorNotes: Grass, straw, leaves, and rootlets are collected and arranged on a secure support.
evidence: much strong grass, fine straw, leaves and rootlets

questions.prompt: How is the nest molded into shape?
facilitatorNotes: A bird sits in the softened material and turns around, using its body to shape it.
evidence: molds it to the body by nestling and turning around and around.

questions.prompt: Does her example prove all robin pairs divide jobs exactly the same way?
facilitatorNotes: No. She carefully introduces that division as one case she watched, not a count of every pair.
evidence: In one case which the author watched

days.title: When the Dark Comes Down
days.challenge: Find how the same repeated time phrase links sea, land, and home.
days.focus: Nightfall transforming work into rest.
days.context: The poem moves from returning fishing boats to a landscape and then to sleeping children.

excerpt.locator: When the Dark Comes Down; complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “When the dark comes down, oh, the wind is on the sea …”; closes “… to frown, And every wave's a lyric when the dark comes down.”.

blocks.text:
When the dark comes down, oh, the wind is on the sea
With lisping laugh and whimper to the red reef's threnody,
The boats are sailing homeward now across the harbor bar
With many a jest and many a shout from fishing grounds afar.
So furl your sails and take your rest, ye fisher folk so brown,
For task and quest are ended when the dark comes down.

When the dark comes down, oh, the landward valleys fill
Like brimming cups of purple, and on every landward hill
There shines a star of twilight that is watching evermore
The low, dim lighted meadows by the long, dim-lighted shore,
For there, where vagrant daisies weave the grass a silver crown,
The lads and lassies wander when the dark comes down.

When the dark comes down, oh, the children fall asleep,
And mothers in the fisher huts their happy vigils keep;
There's music in the song they sing and music on the sea,
The loving, lingering echoes of the twilight's litany,
For toil has folded hands to dream, and care has ceased to frown,
And every wave's a lyric when the dark comes down.

questions.prompt: What tells us the fishing day is ending?
facilitatorNotes: Boats cross the harbor bar toward home and the speaker tells fishers to furl their sails and rest.
evidence: The boats are sailing homeward now

questions.prompt: What shape does the poem give the filling valleys?
facilitatorNotes: They are brimming cups of purple, an image of dusk spreading through low ground.
evidence: Like brimming cups of purple,

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza make care seem to relax like a person?
facilitatorNotes: Care stops frowning and toil folds its hands to dream; these personifications make the whole scene restful.
evidence: care has ceased to frown,

days.title: How the Camel Got His Hump — the extra work (part 1)
days.challenge: Read the repeated reply in dialogue and follow the work assigned to each animal.
days.focus: Refusal shifting a burden onto others.
days.context: The story imagines the early world as a place where animals are first learning their jobs.
days.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. Kipling’s colonial-era narrator uses exaggerated voices and cultural references; these belong to the historical story. Several borrowed cultural names are piled together for the animals’ meeting; they do not represent those cultures accurately.

excerpt.locator: How the Camel Got His Hump — the extra work (part 1); contiguous excerpt, 19 source blocks; opens “NOW this is the next tale, and it tells how the Camel …”; closes “… the Djinn. 'I'll humph him if you will kindly wait a minute.'”.

blocks.text: NOW this is the next tale, and it tells how the Camel got his big hump.

In the beginning of years, when the world was so new and all, and the Animals were just beginning to work for Man, there was a Camel, and he lived in the middle of a Howling Desert because he did not want to work; and besides, he was a Howler himself. So he ate sticks and thorns and tamarisks and milkweed and prickles, most 'scruciating idle; and when anybody spoke to him he said 'Humph!' Just 'Humph!' and no more.
Presently the Horse came to him on Monday morning, with a saddle on his back and a bit in his mouth, and said, 'Camel, O Camel, come out and trot like the rest of us.'
'Humph!' said the Camel; and the Horse went away and told the Man.
Presently the Dog came to him, with a stick in his mouth, and said, 'Camel, O Camel, come and fetch and carry like the rest of us.'
'Humph!' said the Camel; and the Dog went away and told the Man.
Presently the Ox came to him, with the yoke on his neck and said, 'Camel, O Camel, come and plough like the rest of us.'
'Humph!' said the Camel; and the Ox went away and told the Man.

At the end of the day the Man called the Horse and the Dog and the Ox together, and said, 'Three, O Three, I'm very sorry for you (with the world so new-and-all); but that Humph-thing in the Desert can't work, or he would have been here by now, so I am going to leave him alone, and you must work double-time to make up for it.'

That made the Three very angry (with the world so new-and-all), and they held a palaver, and an indaba, and a punchayet, and a pow-wow on the edge of the Desert; and the Camel came chewing milkweed most 'scruciating idle, and laughed at them. Then he said 'Humph!' and went away again.
Presently there came along the Djinn in charge of All Deserts, rolling in a cloud of dust (Djinns always travel that way because it is Magic), and he stopped to palaver and pow-pow with the Three.
'Djinn of All Deserts,' said the Horse, 'is it right for any one to be idle, with the world so new-and-all?'
'Certainly not,' said the Djinn.

'Well,' said the Horse, 'there's a thing in the middle of your Howling Desert (and he's a Howler himself) with a long neck and long legs, and he hasn't done a stroke of work since Monday morning. He won't trot.'
'Whew!' said the Djinn, whistling, 'that's my Camel, for all the gold in Arabia! What does he say about it?'
'He says "Humph!"' said the Dog; 'and he won't fetch and carry.'
'Does he say anything else?'
'Only "Humph!"; and he won't plough,' said the Ox.
'Very good,' said the Djinn. 'I'll humph him if you will kindly wait a minute.'

questions.prompt: How does the Camel answer requests to join the work?
facilitatorNotes: He keeps saying “Humph,” giving no helpful response to the Horse, Dog, or Ox.
evidence: Humph!

questions.prompt: Why are the three working animals angry after speaking to the Man?
facilitatorNotes: Because they must do extra work to make up for the Camel’s refusal.
evidence: work double-time to make up for it.

questions.prompt: Why does meeting the Djinn create a possible change in the story?
facilitatorNotes: He is in charge of deserts and hears the workers’ complaint, so he has both information and imagined power to act.
evidence: Djinn in charge of All Deserts

days.title: How the Camel Got His Hump — a lasting reminder (part 2)
days.challenge: Connect the repeated sound “Humph” with the story’s invented physical consequence.
days.focus: A comic origin story ending in an address to the reader.
days.context: The working animals have complained to the Djinn about the Camel. The Djinn now speaks with him.
days.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. Kipling’s colonial-era narrator uses exaggerated voices and cultural references; these belong to the historical story.

excerpt.locator: How the Camel Got His Hump — a lasting reminder (part 2); contiguous excerpt, 19 source blocks; opens “The Djinn rolled himself up in his dust-cloak, and took a bearing …”; closes “… to do-oo-oo— We all get hump— Cameelious hump— Kiddies and grown-ups too!”.

blocks.text: The Djinn rolled himself up in his dust-cloak, and took a bearing across the desert, and found the Camel most 'scruciatingly idle, looking at his own reflection in a pool of water.
'My long and bubbling friend,' said the Djinn, 'what's this I hear of your doing no work, with the world so new-and-all?'
'Humph!' said the Camel.
The Djinn sat down, with his chin in his hand, and began to think a Great Magic, while the Camel looked at his own reflection in the pool of water.
'You've given the Three extra work ever since Monday morning, all on account of your 'scruciating idleness,' said the Djinn; and he went on thinking Magics, with his chin in his hand.
'Humph!' said the Camel.
'I shouldn't say that again if I were you,' said the Djinn; 'you might say it once too often. Bubbles, I want you to work.'
And the Camel said 'Humph!' again; but no sooner had he said it than he saw his back, that he was so proud of, puffing up and puffing up into a great big lolloping humph.

'Do you see that?' said the Djinn. 'That's your very own humph that you've brought upon your very own self by not working. To-day is Thursday, and you've done no work since Monday, when the work began. Now you are going to work.'
'How can I,' said the Camel, 'with this humph on my back?'

'That's made a-purpose,' said the Djinn, 'all because you missed those three days. You will be able to work now for three days without eating, because you can live on your humph; and don't you ever say I never did anything for you. Come out of the Desert and go to the Three, and behave. Humph yourself!'

And the Camel humphed himself, humph and all, and went away to join the Three. And from that day to this the Camel always wears a humph (we call it 'hump' now, not to hurt his feelings); but he has never yet caught up with the three days that he missed at the beginning of the world, and he has never yet learned how to behave.

The Camel's hump is an ugly lump
Which well you may see at the Zoo;
But uglier yet is the hump we get
From having too little to do.

Kiddies and grown-ups too-oo-oo,
If we haven't enough to do-oo-oo,
We get the hump—
Cameelious hump—
The hump that is black and blue!

We climb out of bed with a frouzly head
And a snarly-yarly voice.
We shiver and scowl and we grunt and we growl
At our bath and our boots and our toys;

And there ought to be a corner for me
(And I know there is one for you)
When we get the hump—
Cameelious hump—
The hump that is black and blue!

And then you will find that the sun and the wind,
And the Djinn of the Garden too,
Have lifted the hump—
The horrible hump—
The hump that is black and blue!

I get it as well as you-oo-oo—
If I haven't enough to do-oo-oo—
We all get hump—
Cameelious hump—
Kiddies and grown-ups too!

questions.prompt: Why can the Camel no longer simply repeat his old answer without consequence?
facilitatorNotes: The Djinn turns his repeated “Humph” into a hump; the verbal joke becomes a bodily change.
evidence: a great big lolloping humph.

questions.prompt: What use does the Djinn claim for the new hump?
facilitatorNotes: It will let the Camel work three days without eating to make up for the time he missed; this is the story’s fantasy, not a biology lesson.
evidence: work now for three days without eating

questions.prompt: How does the closing poem widen the story beyond the Camel?
facilitatorNotes: It addresses children and grown-ups and uses the hump as an image for idleness or bad mood; discuss the narrator’s advice without requiring agreement.
evidence: Kiddies and grown-ups too-oo-oo,

days.title: The Lamb
days.challenge: Separate the first stanza’s questions from the second stanza’s religious answer.
days.focus: A speaker linking gentleness, a child, and a lamb.
days.context: This complete poem uses Christian images, especially the name Lamb for Jesus. Look at how its answer echoes its question.
days.contentNote: This poem expresses the author’s Christian belief. Discuss that viewpoint without asking readers to share it.

excerpt.locator: The Lamb; complete work, 2 source blocks; opens “Little lamb, who made thee? Does thou know who made thee, Gave …”; closes “… His name. Little lamb, God bless thee! Little lamb, God bless thee!”.

blocks.text:
Little lamb, who made thee?
Does thou know who made thee,
Gave thee life, and bid thee feed
By the stream and o’er the mead;
Gave thee clothing of delight,
Softest clothing, woolly, bright;
Gave thee such a tender voice,
Making all the vales rejoice?
Little lamb, who made thee?
Does thou know who made thee?

Little lamb, I’ll tell thee;
Little lamb, I’ll tell thee:
He is callèd by thy name,
For He calls Himself a Lamb.
He is meek, and He is mild,
He became a little child.
I a child, and thou a lamb,
We are callèd by His name.
Little lamb, God bless thee!
Little lamb, God bless thee!

questions.prompt: What does the speaker notice about the lamb before answering who made it?
facilitatorNotes: Food, life, soft wool, and a tender voice; these gentle gifts prepare the poem’s answer.
evidence: Softest clothing, woolly, bright;

questions.prompt: Why is the name Lamb used for more than the animal?
facilitatorNotes: Within the poem’s Christian belief it also names Jesus, who is described as meek, mild, and once a child.
evidence: For He calls Himself a Lamb.

questions.prompt: How do the repeated closing lines differ from the opening repetition?
facilitatorNotes: The opening asks who made the lamb; the ending blesses it. The poem moves from inquiry to affectionate assurance.
evidence: Little lamb, God bless thee!

days.title: A Winter Day
days.challenge: Compare three numbered parts while tracking dawn, noon, and evening.
days.focus: A single winter day with changing moods.
days.context: Read each section with a different pace. “Mere” is a lake and “occidental” means western.
days.contentNote: This poem expresses the author’s Christian belief. Discuss that viewpoint without asking readers to share it.

excerpt.locator: A Winter Day; complete work, 6 source blocks; opens “I”; closes “… Whence priest-like winds on crystal air Summon the reverent world to prayer.”.

blocks.text: I
II
III

Faint music rings in wold and dell,
The tinkling of a distant bell,
Where homestead lights with friendly glow
Glimmer across the drifted snow;
Beyond a valley dim and far
Lit by an occidental star,
Tall pines the marge of day beset
Like many a slender minaret,
Whence priest-like winds on crystal air
Summon the reverent world to prayer.

questions.prompt: What makes the dawn section feel like a beginning?
facilitatorNotes: The waiting white world receives morning, with eastern light and a newly arriving day.
evidence: The morning comes in wonder clad;

questions.prompt: How does noon feel more energetic than evening?
facilitatorNotes: Noon emphasizes jollity, zest, laughter, and courage; evening brings bells, home lights, and prayer.
evidence: Laughter and courage have their way

questions.prompt: What do the distant bell and homestead lights add to the snowy landscape?
facilitatorNotes: They suggest human shelter and community within the wide cold scene; accept evidence-based alternatives about comfort.
evidence:
Where homestead lights with friendly glow
Glimmer across the drifted snow;

days.title: The Moonlight Trails — excerpt: a pattern in the snow
days.challenge: Connect a pattern of footprints with the movements that make it.
days.focus: Stillness, play and watchfulness coexist.
days.context: Roberts opens an animal story in a still winter forest. Read the descriptions aloud, then reread the paragraph in which the rabbits gather.
days.contentNote: Roberts gives the animals thoughts and feelings, a convention of the literary animal story of his time.

excerpt.locator: The Moonlight Trails; contiguous excerpt, 5 source blocks; opens “There was no wind. The young fir-trees stood up straight and tall …”; closes “… Only toward the north side of the open there went not one.”.

blocks.text: There was no wind. The young fir-trees stood up straight and tall and stiffly pointed from the noiseless white levels of the snow. The blue-white moon of midwinter, sharply glittering like an icicle, hung high in a heaven clear as tempered steel.

The young fir-trees were a second growth, on lands once well cleared, but afterward reclaimed by the forest. They rose in serried phalanxes, with here and there a solitary sentinel of spruce, and here and there a little huddling group of yellow birches. The snow-spaces between formed sparkling alleys, and long, mysterious vistas, expanding frequently into amphitheatres of breathless stillness and flooding radiance. There was no trace of that most ghostly and elusive winter haze which represents the fine breathing of the forest. Rather the air seemed like diamonds held in solution, fluent as by miracle, and not without strange peril to be jarred by sound or motion.

Yet presently the exaggerated tension of the stillness was broken, and no disaster followed. Two small, white, furry shapes came leaping, one behind the other, down a corridor of radiance, as lightly as if a wind were lifting and drifting them. It was as if some of the gentler spirits of the winter and the wild had seized the magic hour for an incarnation. Leaping at gay leisure, their little bodies would lengthen out to a span of nearly three feet, then round themselves together so that the soft pads of their hinder paws would touch the snow within a couple of inches of the prints from which their fore paws were even then starting to rise. The trail thus drawn down the white aisle consisted of an orderly succession of close triplicate bunches of footprints, like no other trail of the wild folk. From time to time the two harmonious shapes would halt, sit up on their hindquarters, erect their long, attentive ears, glance about warily with their bulging eyes which, in this position, could see behind as well as in front of their narrow heads, wrinkle those cleft nostrils which were cunning to differentiate every scent upon the sharp air, and then browse hastily but with a cheerful relish at the spicy shoots of the young yellow birch. Feeding, however, was plainly not their chief purpose. Always within a few moments they would resume their leaping progress through the white glitter and the hard, black shadows.

Very soon their path led them out into a wide glade, fenced all about with the serried and formal ranks of the young firs. It seemed as if the blue-white moon stared down into this space with a glassiness of brilliance even more deluding and magical than elsewhere. The snow here was crossed by a tangle of the fine triplicate tracks. Doubling upon themselves in all directions and with obvious irresponsibility, they were evidently the trails of play rather than of business or of flight. Their pattern was the pattern of mirth; and some half dozen wild white rabbits were gaily weaving at it when the two newcomers joined them. Long ears twinkling, round eyes softly shining, they leaped lightly hither and thither, pausing every now and then to touch each other with their sensitive noses, or to pound on the snow with their strong hind legs in mock challenge. It seemed to be the play of care-free children, almost a kind of confused dance, a spontaneous expression of the joy of life. Nevertheless, for all the mirth of it, there was never a moment when two or more of the company were not to be seen sitting erect, with watchful ears and eyes, close in the shadow of the young fir-trees. For the night that was so favourable to the wild rabbits was favourable also to the fox, the wildcat, and the weasel. And death stalks joy forever among the kindred of the wild.

From time to time one or another of the leaping players would take himself off through the fir-trees, while others continued to arrive along the moonlight trails. This went on till the moon had swung perhaps an hour’s distance on her shining course; then, suddenly it stopped; and just for a fleeting fraction of a breath all the players were motionless, with ears one way. From one or another of the watchers there had come some signal, swift, but to the rabbits instantly clear. No onlooker not of the cleft-nose, long-ear clan could have told in what the signal consisted, or what was its full significance. But whatever it was, in a moment the players were gone, vanishing to the east and west and south, all at once, as if blown off by a mighty breath. Only toward the north side of the open there went not one.

questions.prompt: Which details make the opening feel unusually still?
facilitatorNotes: There is no wind, the trees stand stiffly, and the air seems fragile. Choose particular words rather than just saying it is quiet.
evidence: There was no wind.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator call the tracks in the clearing signs of play?
facilitatorNotes: They double back and cross in many directions, unlike a direct journey. The rabbits’ movements confirm the interpretation.
evidence: the trails of play rather than of business or of flight

questions.prompt: What shows that playing has not made the rabbits completely careless?
