days.title: The Paradise of Children — excerpt: another knock
days.challenge: Compare a decision made after harm with the earlier decision made before it.
days.focus: A gentle voice begins to interrupt fear and blame.
days.context: Troubles have escaped from the box and hurt both children. A new voice now asks to be let out.

excerpt.locator: A Wonder Book; contiguous excerpt, 18 source blocks; opens “Meanwhile, the naughty Pandora, and hardly less naughty Epimetheus, remained in their …”; closes “"You might speak a little more kindly!" murmured Pandora, wiping her eyes.”.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the naughty Pandora, and hardly less naughty Epimetheus, remained in their cottage. Both of them had been grievously stung, and were in a good deal of pain, which seemed the more intolerable to them, because it was the very first pain that had ever been felt since the world began. Of course, they were entirely unaccustomed to it, and could have no idea what it meant. Besides all this, they were in exceedingly bad humor, both with themselves and with one another. In order to indulge it to the utmost, Epimetheus sat down sullenly in a corner with his back towards Pandora; while Pandora flung herself upon the floor and rested her head on the fatal and abominable box. She was crying bitterly, and sobbing as if her heart would break.
Suddenly there was a gentle little tap on the inside of the lid.
"What can that be?" cried Pandora, lifting her head.
But either Epimetheus had not heard the tap, or was too much out of humor to notice it. At any rate, he made no answer.
"You are very unkind," said Pandora, sobbing anew, "not to speak to me!"
Again the tap! It sounded like the tiny knuckles of a fairy's hand, knocking lightly and playfully on the inside of the box.
"Who are you?" asked Pandora, with a little of her former curiosity. "Who are you, inside of this naughty box?"
A sweet little voice spoke from within,—
"Only lift the lid, and you shall see."

"No, no," answered Pandora, again beginning to sob, "I have had enough of lifting the lid! You are inside of the box, naughty creature, and there you shall stay! There are plenty of your ugly brothers and sisters already flying about the world. You need never think that I shall be so foolish as to let you out!"
She looked towards Epimetheus, as she spoke, perhaps expecting that he would commend her for her wisdom. But the sullen boy only muttered that she was wise a little too late.

"Ah," said the sweet little voice again, "you had much better let me out. I am not like those naughty creatures that have stings in their tails. They are no brothers and sisters of mine, as you would see at once, if you were only to get a glimpse of me. Come, come, my pretty Pandora! I am sure you will let me out!"

And, indeed, there was a kind of cheerful witchery in the tone, that made it almost impossible to refuse anything which this little voice asked. Pandora's heart had insensibly grown lighter, at every word that came from within the box. Epimetheus, too, though still in the corner, had turned half round, and seemed to be in rather better spirits than before.
"My dear Epimetheus," cried Pandora, "have you heard this little voice?"
"Yes, to be sure I have," answered he, but in no very good-humor as yet. "And what of it?"
"Shall I lift the lid again?" asked Pandora.

"Just as you please," said Epimetheus. "You have done so much mischief already, that perhaps you may as well do a little more. One other Trouble, in such a swarm as you have set adrift about the world, can make no very great difference."
"You might speak a little more kindly!" murmured Pandora, wiping her eyes.

days.title: The Paradise of Children — excerpt: the last guest
days.challenge: Interpret a personified idea through its appearance, actions and promises.
days.focus: Hope does not erase trouble but helps the children face it.
days.context: A gentle voice remains inside the box. Pandora and Epimetheus must decide together whether to release it.
days.contentNote: The myth closes with the storyteller’s faith in a future happiness. Present that as this narrator’s belief and allow different family beliefs; Hope is a fictional personification.

excerpt.locator: A Wonder Book; contiguous excerpt, 15 source blocks; opens “"Ah, naughty boy!" cried the little voice within the box, in an …”; closes “… shows it to be only the shadow of an infinite bliss hereafter!”.

blocks.text: "Ah, naughty boy!" cried the little voice within the box, in an arch and laughing tone. "He knows he is longing to see me. Come, my dear Pandora, lift up the lid. I am in a great hurry to comfort you. Only let me have some fresh air, and you shall soon see that matters are not quite so dismal as you think them!"
"Epimetheus," exclaimed Pandora, "come what may, I am resolved to open the box!"
"And, as the lid seems very heavy," cried Epimetheus, running across the room, "I will help you!"

So, with one consent, the two children again lifted the lid. Out flew a sunny and smiling little personage, and hovered about the room, throwing a light wherever she went. Have you never made the sunshine dance into dark corners, by reflecting it from a bit of looking-glass? Well, so looked the winged cheerfulness of this fairy-like stranger, amid the gloom of the cottage. She flew to Epimetheus, and laid the least touch of her finger on the inflamed spot where the Trouble had stung him, and immediately the anguish of it was gone. Then she kissed Pandora on the forehead, and her hurt was cured likewise.

After performing these good offices, the bright stranger fluttered sportively over the children's heads, and looked so sweetly at them, that they both began to think it not so very much amiss to have opened the box, since, otherwise, their cheery guest must have been kept a prisoner among those naughty imps with stings in their tails.
"Pray, who are you, beautiful creature?" inquired Pandora.

"I am to be called Hope!" answered the sunshiny figure. "And because I am such a cheery little body, I was packed into the box, to make amends to the human race for that swarm of ugly Troubles, which was destined to be let loose among them. Never fear! we shall do pretty well in spite of them all."
"Your wings are colored like the rainbow!" exclaimed Pandora. "How very beautiful!"
"Yes, they are like the rainbow," said Hope, "because, glad as my nature is, I am partly made of tears as well as smiles."
"And will you stay with us," asked Epimetheus, "forever and ever?"

"As long as you need me," said Hope, with her pleasant smile,—"and that will be as long as you live in the world,—I promise never to desert you. There may come times and seasons, now and then, when you will think that I have utterly vanished. But again, and again, and again, when perhaps you least dream of it, you shall see the glimmer of my wings on the ceiling of your cottage. Yes, my dear children, and I know something very good and beautiful that is to be given you hereafter!"
"Oh tell us," they exclaimed,—"tell us what it is!"
"Do not ask me," replied Hope, putting her finger on her rosy mouth. "But do not despair, even if it should never happen while you live on this earth. Trust in my promise, for it is true."
"We do trust you!" cried Epimetheus and Pandora, both in one breath.

And so they did; and not only they, but so has everybody trusted Hope, that has since been alive. And to tell you the truth, I cannot help being glad—(though, to be sure, it was an uncommonly naughty thing for her to do)—but I cannot help being glad that our foolish Pandora peeped into the box. No doubt—no doubt—the Troubles are still flying about the world, and have increased in multitude, rather than lessened, and are a very ugly set of imps, and carry most venomous stings in their tails. I have felt them already, and expect to feel them more, as I grow older. But then that lovely and lightsome little figure of Hope! What in the world could we do without her? Hope spiritualizes the earth; Hope makes it always new; and, even in the earth's best and brightest aspect, Hope shows it to be only the shadow of an infinite bliss hereafter!

facilitatorNotes: Epimetheus agrees to help, so the action is openly shared. The scene replaces secret action and blame with cooperation.

facilitatorNotes: Hope can coexist with sorrow; it is not a promise that everything is already pleasant. Connect this with her rainbow-like appearance.
evidence: I am partly made of tears as well as smiles.

facilitatorNotes: She promises not to desert them even when she seems absent. Treat this as the story’s personification, and invite discussion of a small action that could express it.

days.title: The White Clover — carpet and flower-head (excerpt)
days.challenge: Use two paragraphs to connect stem, leaf, and flower structure.
days.focus: Many small parts making a familiar lawn plant.
days.context: Read the opening comparison with sweet clover as orientation; the selected explanation then describes white clover itself.

excerpt.locator: The White Clover — carpet and flower-head (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 2 source blocks; opens “THE sweet clover should be studied first, for after making this study …”; closes “… as the florets are pollenated they wither and droop below the flower-head.”.

blocks.text: THE sweet clover should be studied first, for after making this study it is easier to understand the blossoming of the white and the red clover. In the sweet clovers, the flowers are strung along the stalk but in the red, the white, and many others, it is as if the blossom stalk were telescoped, so that the flowers are all in one bunch, the tip of the stalk making the center of the clover head. We use the white clover in our lawns because of a peculiarity of its stem, which, instead of standing erect, lies flat on the ground, sending leaves and blossoms upward and thus making a thick carpet over the ground. The leaves are very pretty; and although they grow upon the stems alternately, they always manage to twist around so as to lift their three leaflets upward to the light. The three leaflets are nearly equal in size, with fine, even veins and toothed edges; and each has upon it, near the middle a pale, angular spot. The white clover, in common with other clovers, has the pretty habit of going to sleep at night. Botanists may object to this human term, but the great Linnæus first called it sleep, and we may be permitted to follow his example. Certainly the way the clover leaves fold at the middle, the three drawing near each other, looks like going to sleep, and is one of the things which even the little child will enjoy observing.

The clover head is made up of many little flowers; each one has a tubular calyx with five delicate points and a little stem to hold it up into the world. In shape, the corolla is much like that of the sweet pea, and each secretes nectar at its base. The outside blossoms open first; and as soon as open, the honey bees, which eagerly visit white clover wherever it is growing, begin at once their work of gathering nectar and carrying pollen; as soon as the florets are pollenated they wither and droop below the flower-head.

days.title: The Call of the Winds
days.challenge: Compare four seasonal speakers and explain their different invitations.
days.focus: The year offering several kinds of renewal.
days.context: Each stanza speaks as a wind from a different season. Assign four voices before discussing what stays alike.

excerpt.locator: The Call of the Winds; complete work, 4 source blocks; opens “Ho, come out with the wind of spring, And step it blithely …”; closes “… hearts are sad, I will make you valiant and strong and glad!”.

blocks.text:
Ho, come out with the wind of spring,
And step it blithely in woodlands waking;
Friend am I of each growing thing
From the gray sod into sunshine breaking;
Mine is the magic of twilights dim,
Of violets blue on the still pool's rim,
Mine is the breath of the blossoms young
Sweetest of fragrances storied or sung—
Come, ye earth-children, weary and worn,
I will lead you over the hills of morn.

Ho, come out with the summer wind,
And loiter in meadows of ripening clover,
Where the purple noons are long and kind,
And the great white clouds drift fleecily over.
Mine is immortal minstrelsy,
The fellowship of the rose and bee,
Beguiling laughter of willowed rills,
The rejoicing of pines on inland hills,
Come, ye earth-children, by dale and stream,
I will lead you into the ways of dream.

Ho, when the wind of autumn rings
Through jubilant mornings crisp and golden,
Come where the yellow woodland flings
Its hoarded wealth over by-ways olden.
Mine are the grasses frosted and sere,
That lisp and rustle around the mere,
Mine are the flying racks that dim
The lingering sunset's reddening rim,
Earth-children, come, in the waning year,
I will harp you to laughter and buoyant cheer.

Ho, when the wind of winter blows
Over the uplands and moonlit spaces,
Come ye out to the waste of snows,
To the glimmering fields and the silent places.
I whistle gaily on starry nights
Through the arch of the elfin northern lights,
But in long white valleys I pause to hark
Where the ring of the home-lights gems the dark.
Come, ye earth-children, whose hearts are sad,
I will make you valiant and strong and glad!

questions.prompt: How do the spring and summer invitations differ?
facilitatorNotes: Spring calls readers to lively growing woodlands and morning hills; summer invites slower movement and dreams in meadows.
evidence: And loiter in meadows of ripening clover,

questions.prompt: What image makes autumn leaves seem valuable?
facilitatorNotes: The woodland flings hoarded wealth over the paths, turning fallen yellow leaves into treasure.
evidence: Its hoarded wealth over by-ways olden.

questions.prompt: What common promise remains even in winter?
facilitatorNotes: The winds offer companionship, courage, or joy to weary or sad people; winter explicitly promises strength and gladness.
evidence: I will make you valiant and strong and glad!

days.title: The Christmas Fern — a record of earlier years (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow several time layers in one paragraph without confusing stem and root.
days.focus: Old growth as evidence of a living plant’s history.
days.context: A rootstock is a stem, and a frond is a fern leaf. Read with an adult and draw a growing tip plus the remains behind it.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Fern — a record of earlier years (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 1 source blocks; opens “The rootstock of the fern is an humble example of “rising on …”; closes “… gradually die down, leaving it rough below its crown of green plumes.”.

blocks.text: The rootstock of the fern is an humble example of “rising on stepping stones of our dead selves,” this being almost literally true of the tree-ferns. The rootstock which is a stem and not a root—has, like other stems, a growing tip from which, each year, it sends up into the world several beautiful green fronds, and numerous rootlets down into the earth. These graceful fronds rejoice the world and our eyes for the summer, and make glad the one who, in winter, loves to wander often in the woods to inquire after the welfare of his many friends during their period of sleeping and waking. These fronds, after giving their message of winter cheer, and after the following summer has made the whole woodland green and the young fronds are growing thriftily from the tip of the rootstock, die down, and in midsummer we can find the old fronds lying sere and brown, with broken stipes, just back of the new fern clump; if we examine the rootstock we can detect behind them, remains of the stems of the fronds of year before last; and still farther behind we may trace all the stems of fronds which gladdened the world three years ago. Thus we learn that this rootstock may have been creeping on an inch or so each season for many years, always busy with the present and giving no heed to its dead past. One of the chief differences between our ferns and the tree-ferns of the tropics, which we often see in greenhouses, is that in the tree-fern the rootstock rises in the air instead of creeping on, or below, the surface of the ground. This upright rootstock of the tree-fern also bears fronds at its tip, and its old fronds gradually die down, leaving it rough below its crown of green plumes.

questions.prompt: Why does the author insist that the rootstock is a stem?
facilitatorNotes: It has a growing tip that sends fronds upward and rootlets downward; its position near the ground does not make it a root.
evidence: The rootstock which is a stem and not a root

questions.prompt: How can a reader imagine tracing more than one previous year?
facilitatorNotes: Behind the newest clump are old brown fronds and older stem remains, creating a sequence of past growth.
evidence: we may trace all the stems of fronds which gladdened the world three years ago.

questions.prompt: What major difference does the passage draw between these ferns and tropical tree-ferns?
facilitatorNotes: The tree-fern’s rootstock rises in the air instead of creeping at or below ground level; both bear new fronds at the tip.
evidence: the rootstock rises in the air instead of creeping on, or below, the surface of the ground.

days.title: The Sunflower — a procession of bloom (excerpt)
days.challenge: Use spatial words to trace a flower-head from outside toward its center.
days.focus: Repeated observation revealing change.
days.context: Return to the earlier sunflower idea: one head contains many small flowers. Bracts are leaflike structures surrounding the head. A partner can explain corolla, stigma, and anther as flower parts while you follow the arrangement from the edge inward. This passage asks for patient looking across several days.

excerpt.locator: The Sunflower — a procession of bloom (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 2 source blocks; opens “But more wonderful than the perfection of each floret is their arrangement …”; closes “… and each bract is bent so as to fit around the disk.”.

blocks.text: But more wonderful than the perfection of each floret is their arrangement in the flower-head. Around the edge of the disk the banner-flowers, in double or treble rank, flare wide their long petals like the rays of the sun, making the sunflower a most striking object in the landscape. If the sunflower has been open for several days, next to the ray-flowers will be seen a circle of star-mouthed corollas from which both ripened pollen and stigmas have disappeared, and the fertilized seeds below them are attaining their growth. Next comes a two or three-ranked circle, where the split, coiled-back stigma-lobes protrude from the anther-tubes; within this circle may be two or three rows of florets, where pollen is being pushed out in starry radiance; and within this ring there may be a circle where the anther-tubes are still closed; while at the center lie the buds, arranged in exquisite pattern of circling radii, cut by radii circling in the opposite direction; and at the very center the buds are covered with the green spear-points of their bracts. I never look at the buds in the sunflower without wondering if the study of their arrangement is not the basis of much of the most exquisite decoration in Moorish architecture. To appreciate fully this procession of the bloom of the sunflower from its rim to its center, we need to watch it day by day—then only can its beauty become a part of us.

The great, green bracts, with their long pointed tips, which “shingle” the house of every sunflower family, should be noted with care, because these bracts have manifold forms in the great Compositæ family; and the pupil should learn to recognize this part of the flower-head, merely from its position. In the burdocks, these bracts form the hooks which fasten to the passer-by; in the thistle, they form the prickly vase about the blossom; while in the pearly everlasting, they make the beautiful, white, shell-like mass of the flower which we treasure as immortal. In the sunflower, these bracts are very ornamental, being feltlike outside and very smooth inside, bordered with fringes of pretty hairs, which may be seen best through a lens. They overlap each other regularly in circular rows, and each bract is bent so as to fit around the disk.

questions.prompt: Which part forms the bright outer edge?
facilitatorNotes: Ray or banner flowers spread long petals around the disk like sun rays.
evidence: flare wide their long petals like the rays of the sun,

questions.prompt: Why does the author say one glance is not enough to appreciate the bloom?
facilitatorNotes: Different rings show different stages, and the procession moves inward over time; repeated observation reveals that process.
evidence: we need to watch it day by day

questions.prompt: Why compare the green bracts with shingles on a house?
facilitatorNotes: They overlap in orderly rows around the flower-head, suggesting layered protection like a roof.
evidence: They overlap each other regularly in circular rows,

days.title: The Sunflower — releasing the seeds (excerpt)
days.challenge: Explain a chain of causes using a compact scientific description.
days.focus: A bending head helping seeds scatter.
days.context: This final nature paragraph connects birds, loosened seeds, a bending stem, and autumn wind. Reread independently, then justify the sequence.

excerpt.locator: The Sunflower — releasing the seeds (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 1 source blocks; opens “The sunflower seed is eagerly sought by many birds, and it is …”; closes “… the bended heads shake out their seed and scatter them far afield.”.

blocks.text: The sunflower seed is eagerly sought by many birds, and it is raised extensively for chicken-feed. The inadequate little pappus falls off, and the seeds are set, large end up, in the very ornamental diamond-shaped sockets. They finally become loosened, and now we see a reason for the bending flower-head; for, as the great stem is assaulted by the winds of autumn, the bended heads shake out their seed and scatter them far afield.

questions.prompt: Who seeks the seeds before they fall?
facilitatorNotes: Many birds seek them, and people also grow sunflower seed for chickens.
evidence: eagerly sought by many birds,

questions.prompt: What change must happen before the head can easily release its seeds?
facilitatorNotes: The seeds become loosened in their sockets; their earlier firm placement changes.
evidence: They finally become loosened,

questions.prompt: How do the wind and the bent head work together?
facilitatorNotes: Wind shakes the stem, and the downward-bent heads shake out and scatter the loosened seeds.
evidence: the bended heads shake out their seed and scatter them far afield.

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy — excerpt: news travels through the village
days.challenge: Trace how one event becomes a story many people repeat.
days.focus: Curiosity changes the ordinary routines of a community.
days.context: Cedric, an American boy, has learned that he is heir to an English earldom. He lives with his grandfather at the Castle while his mother lives nearby. He has recently asked for help for a tenant named Higgins.
days.contentNote: The story turns on English inherited rank, property and domestic service in the 1880s, which Burnett sets against Cedric’s American upbringing. Cedric’s father has died before these events.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII.; contiguous excerpt, 6 source blocks; opens “On the following Sunday morning, Mr. Mordaunt had a large congregation. Indeed, …”; closes “… lord who was to be in time the owner of the soil.”.

blocks.text: On the following Sunday morning, Mr. Mordaunt had a large congregation. Indeed, he could scarcely remember any Sunday on which the church had been so crowded. People appeared upon the scene who seldom did him the honor of coming to hear his sermons. There were even people from Hazelton, which was the next parish. There were hearty, sunburned farmers, stout, comfortable, apple-cheeked wives in their best bonnets and most gorgeous shawls, and half a dozen children or so to each family. The doctor's wife was there, with her four daughters. Mrs. Kimsey and Mr. Kimsey, who kept the druggist's shop, and made pills, and did up powders for everybody within ten miles, sat in their pew; Mrs. Dibble in hers, Miss Smiff, the village dressmaker, and her friend Miss Perkins, the milliner, sat in theirs; the doctor's young man was present, and the druggist's apprentice; in fact, almost every family on the county side was represented, in one way or another.

In the course of the preceding week, many wonderful stories had been told of little Lord Fauntleroy. Mrs. Dibble had been kept so busy attending to customers who came in to buy a pennyworth of needles or a ha'p'orth of tape and to hear what she had to relate, that the little shop bell over the door had nearly tinkled itself to death over the coming and going. Mrs. Dibble knew exactly how his small lordship's rooms had been furnished for him, what expensive toys had been bought, how there was a beautiful brown pony awaiting him, and a small groom to attend it, and a little dog-cart, with silver-mounted harness. And she could tell, too, what all the servants had said when they had caught glimpses of the child on the night of his arrival; and how every female below stairs had said it was a shame, so it was, to part the poor pretty dear from his mother; and had all declared their hearts came into their mouths when he went alone into the library to see his grandfather, for "there was no knowing how he'd be treated, and his lordship's temper was enough to fluster them with old heads on their shoulders, let alone a child."

"But if you'll believe me, Mrs. Jennifer, mum," Mrs. Dibble had said, "fear that child does not know—so Mr. Thomas hisself says; an' set an' smile he did, an' talked to his lordship as if they'd been friends ever since his first hour. An' the Earl so took aback, Mr. Thomas says, that he couldn't do nothing but listen and stare from under his eyebrows. An' it's Mr. Thomas's opinion, Mrs. Bates, mum, that bad as he is, he was pleased in his secret soul, an' proud, too; for a handsomer little fellow, or with better manners, though so old-fashioned, Mr. Thomas says he'd never wish to see."

And then there had come the story of Higgins. The Reverend Mr. Mordaunt had told it at his own dinner table, and the servant who had heard it had told it in the kitchen, and from there it had spread like wildfire.

And on market-day, when Higgins had appeared in town, he had been questioned on every side, and Newick had been questioned too, and in response had shown to two or three people the note signed "Fauntleroy."

And so the farmers' wives had found plenty to talk of over their tea and their shopping, and they had done the subject full justice and made the most of it. And on Sunday they had either walked to church or had been driven in their gigs by their husbands, who were perhaps a trifle curious themselves about the new little lord who was to be in time the owner of the soil.

questions.prompt: What is unusual about the congregation this Sunday?
facilitatorNotes: It includes people who rarely attend and people from another parish. The opening supplies evidence of unusual interest before explaining it.
evidence: People appeared upon the scene who seldom did him the honor

questions.prompt: Why are so many customers buying tiny inexpensive things at Mrs. Dibble’s shop?
facilitatorNotes: Purchases give them an occasion to hear her news about Cedric. The lively bell marks social curiosity as well as trade.
evidence: to hear what she had to relate

questions.prompt: How does news about Higgins travel beyond the first conversation?
facilitatorNotes: It passes from a dinner table to servants and the kitchen, then spreads further. Ask the child to trace the steps and distinguish them from eyewitness knowledge.
evidence: the servant who had heard it had told it in the kitchen

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy — excerpt: a welcome his mother did not expect
days.challenge: Infer a feeling from a sequence of gestures and changing interpretations.
days.focus: A surprising public welcome becomes a personal kindness.
days.context: Villagers wait outside church to see Cedric and the Earl. Cedric’s mother arrives separately, thinking about her son rather than the people around her. Read the long final paragraph together, pausing when her understanding changes.
days.contentNote: The widow’s cap and black clothes refer to the earlier death of Cedric’s father. Bowing to people of high social rank is a custom in the story’s setting, not a present-day requirement.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII.; contiguous excerpt, 5 source blocks; opens “It was by no means the Earl's habit to attend church, but …”; closes “… tall liveried servants, bowled around the corner and down the green lane.”.

blocks.text: It was by no means the Earl's habit to attend church, but he chose to appear on this first Sunday—it was his whim to present himself in the huge family pew, with Fauntleroy at his side.

There were many loiterers in the churchyard, and many lingerers in the lane that morning. There were groups at the gates and in the porch, and there had been much discussion as to whether my lord would really appear or not. When this discussion was at its height, one good woman suddenly uttered an exclamation.
"Eh," she said; "that must be the mother, pretty young thing."

All who heard turned and looked at the slender figure in black coming up the path. The veil was thrown back from her face and they could see how fair and sweet it was, and how the bright hair curled as softly as a child's under the little widow's cap.

She was not thinking of the people about; she was thinking of Cedric, and of his visits to her, and his joy over his new pony, on which he had actually ridden to her door the day before, sitting very straight and looking very proud and happy. But soon she could not help being attracted by the fact that she was being looked at and that her arrival had created some sort of sensation. She first noticed it because an old woman in a red cloak made a bobbing curtsy to her, and then another did the same thing and said, "God bless you, my lady!" and one man after another took off his hat as she passed. For a moment she did not understand, and then she realized that it was because she was little Lord Fauntleroy's mother that they did so, and she flushed rather shyly and smiled and bowed too, and said, "Thank you" in a gentle voice to the old woman who had blessed her. To a person who had always lived in a bustling, crowded American city this simple deference was very novel, and at first just a little embarrassing; but after all, she could not help liking and being touched by the friendly warm-heartedness of which it seemed to speak. She had scarcely passed through the stone porch into the church before the great event of the day happened. The carriage from the Castle, with its handsome horses and tall liveried servants, bowled around the corner and down the green lane.

questions.prompt: Why is the Earl’s planned appearance an event for the villagers?
facilitatorNotes: He does not usually attend, and people are unsure whether he will come.
evidence: It was by no means the Earl's habit to attend church

questions.prompt: What is Cedric’s mother thinking about before she notices the crowd’s response?
facilitatorNotes: Her son’s visits and his pleasure in the pony occupy her thoughts. She is not seeking attention.
evidence: she was thinking of Cedric, and of his visits to her

questions.prompt: Why does her first embarrassment become a warmer feeling?
facilitatorNotes: She recognises that the bows and greetings convey friendly feeling toward her as Cedric’s mother.
evidence: the friendly warm-heartedness of which it seemed to speak

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy — brief excerpt: whom are they greeting?
days.challenge: Use the correction in dialogue to revise a character’s first explanation.
days.focus: The boy thinks first about his grandfather, then discovers his own public role.
days.context: The Earl’s carriage has reached the church. Cedric steps out first, ready to help his grandfather. Try reading this short dialogue independently, then reread it aloud with an adult taking the Earl’s lines.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII.; contiguous excerpt, 9 source blocks; opens “"Here they come!" went from one looker-on to another.”; closes “… old woman who had spoken to his mother; "long life to you!"”.

blocks.text: "Here they come!" went from one looker-on to another.
And then the carriage drew up, and Thomas stepped down and opened the door, and a little boy, dressed in black velvet, and with a splendid mop of bright waving hair, jumped out.
Every man, woman, and child looked curiously upon him.
"He's the Captain over again!" said those of the on-lookers who remembered his father. "He's the Captain's self, to the life!"

He stood there in the sunlight looking up at the Earl, as Thomas helped that nobleman out, with the most affectionate interest that could be imagined. The instant he could help, he put out his hand and offered his shoulder as if he had been seven feet high. It was plain enough to every one that however it might be with other people, the Earl of Dorincourt struck no terror into the breast of his grandson.
"Just lean on me," they heard him say. "How glad the people are to see you, and how well they all seem to know you!"
"Take off your cap, Fauntleroy," said the Earl. "They are bowing to you."
"To me!" cried Fauntleroy, whipping off his cap in a moment, baring his bright head to the crowd and turning shining, puzzled eyes on them as he tried to bow to every one at once.
"God bless your lordship!" said the curtsying, red-cloaked old woman who had spoken to his mother; "long life to you!"

questions.prompt: Why do some onlookers call Cedric “the Captain over again”?
facilitatorNotes: He resembles his late father, whom they remember. It is a comparison, not a claim that he has the same job.
evidence: those of the on-lookers who remembered his father

questions.prompt: What does the phrase about being seven feet high show about Cedric’s offer to help?
facilitatorNotes: His eagerness is greater than his physical size; he offers support as confidently as a much larger person.
evidence: as if he had been seven feet high

questions.prompt: How does Cedric’s understanding of the bows change?
facilitatorNotes: He first thinks people are greeting the Earl; the Earl tells him the bows are for him, and he quickly removes his cap.
evidence: They are bowing to you.

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy — excerpt: a very old way of spelling
days.challenge: Recognise how a child’s joke connects a new discovery with his own experience.
days.focus: Curiosity and music make an unfamiliar place feel welcoming.
days.context: Cedric and the Earl take their places in church. Cedric can see his mother across the room, and he notices two old stone figures beside the family pew.
days.contentNote: The scene includes Christian worship, a memorial inscription and a mother’s prayer. Present these as the family’s practices and beliefs. “Here lyethe” means “Here lies”; the unusual spellings are preserved.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII.; contiguous excerpt, 7 source blocks; opens “"Thank you, ma'am," said Fauntleroy. And then they went into the church, …”; closes “… many soft anxious thoughts in her tender heart in those new days.”.

blocks.text: "Thank you, ma'am," said Fauntleroy. And then they went into the church, and were looked at there, on their way up the aisle to the square, red-cushioned and curtained pew. When Fauntleroy was fairly seated he made two discoveries which pleased him: the first was that, across the church where he could look at her, his mother sat and smiled at him; the second, that at one end of the pew against the wall, knelt two quaint figures carven in stone, facing each other as they kneeled on either side of a pillar supporting two stone missals, their pointed hands folded as if in prayer, their dress very antique and strange. On the tablet by them was written something of which he could only read the curious words:
"Here lyethe ye bodye of Gregorye Arthure Fyrst Earle of Dorincort allsoe of Alysone Hildegarde hys wyfe."
"May I whisper?" inquired his lordship, devoured by curiosity.
"What is it?" said his grandfather.
"Who are they?"
"Some of your ancestors," answered the Earl, "who lived a few hundred years ago."

"Perhaps," said Lord Fauntleroy, regarding them with respect, "perhaps I got my spelling from them." And then he proceeded to find his place in the church service. When the music began, he stood up and looked across at his mother, smiling. He was very fond of music, and his mother and he often sang together, so he joined in with the rest, his pure, sweet, high voice rising as clear as the song of a bird. He quite forgot himself in his pleasure in it. The Earl forgot himself a little too, as he sat in his curtain-shielded corner of the pew and watched the boy. Cedric stood with the big psalter open in his hands, singing with all his childish might, his face a little uplifted, happily; and as he sang, a long ray of sunshine crept in and, slanting through a golden pane of a stained glass window, brightened the falling hair about his young head. His mother, as she looked at him across the church, felt a thrill pass through her heart, and a prayer rose in it too; a prayer that the pure, simple happiness of his childish soul might last, and that the strange, great fortune which had fallen to him might bring no wrong or evil with it. There were many soft anxious thoughts in her tender heart in those new days.

questions.prompt: What two discoveries first please Cedric inside the church?
facilitatorNotes: He can see his mother, and he finds the carved figures interesting. Both draw his attention beyond the grand seat.
evidence: he made two discoveries which pleased him

questions.prompt: Why does Cedric joke that he may have inherited his spelling?
facilitatorNotes: The inscription uses forms that look strange to him; he links his own spelling difficulties to his ancestors. Explain that historical spellings were not simply mistakes.
evidence: perhaps I got my spelling from them

questions.prompt: What does his mother hope while watching him sing?
facilitatorNotes: She hopes his happiness and goodness will survive his new wealth. Her worry shows that fortune can bring responsibilities and risks, not only pleasure.
evidence: might bring no wrong or evil with it

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy — brief excerpt: what matters more than fortune
days.challenge: Follow a brief backward look in time and distinguish a child’s belief from the narrator’s uncertainty.
days.focus: Goodness is measured by how a life affects other people.
days.context: While watching Cedric in church, the narrator recalls what his mother said the night before. Cedric later repeated her advice to his grandfather, whom he believes to be kinder than his reputation suggests.
days.contentNote: The passage recalls the Earl’s estrangement from his late son and prejudice against his son’s wife. Explain “the unforgiven dead” as a reference to that son; it is not a judgment on the child.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII.; contiguous excerpt, 6 source blocks; opens “"Oh, Ceddie!" she had said to him the evening before, as she …”; closes “… bitter, or softened a little, it would have been hard to discover.”.

blocks.text: "Oh, Ceddie!" she had said to him the evening before, as she hung over him in saying good-night, before he went away; "oh, Ceddie, dear, I wish for your sake I was very clever and could say a great many wise things! But only be good, dear, only be brave, only be kind and true always, and then you will never hurt any one, so long as you live, and you may help many, and the big world may be better because my little child was born. And that is best of all, Ceddie,—it is better than everything else, that the world should be a little better because a man has lived—even ever so little better, dearest."
And on his return to the Castle, Fauntleroy had repeated her words to his grandfather.
"And I thought about you when she said that," he ended; "and I told her that was the way the world was because you had lived, and I was going to try if I could be like you."
"And what did she say to that?" asked his lordship, a trifle uneasily.
"She said that was right, and we must always look for good in people and try to be like it."

Perhaps it was this the old man remembered as he glanced through the divided folds of the red curtain of his pew. Many times he looked over the people's heads to where his son's wife sat alone, and he saw the fair face the unforgiven dead had loved, and the eyes which were so like those of the child at his side; but what his thoughts were, and whether they were hard and bitter, or softened a little, it would have been hard to discover.

questions.prompt: What does Cedric’s mother say would matter more than all the grand things in his new life?
facilitatorNotes: Making the world a little better by being good, brave, kind and true. Ask the child to explain the effect she hopes for, not merely recite the adjectives.
evidence: the world should be a little better because a man has lived

questions.prompt: Why might the Earl feel uneasy when Cedric says he wants to be like him?
facilitatorNotes: The boy’s trust presents a kinder picture than the Earl’s past conduct. The context and his uneasy response support this inference.
evidence: a trifle uneasily

questions.prompt: Can readers be certain the Earl’s feelings toward Cedric’s mother have changed?
facilitatorNotes: No. The narrator explicitly leaves his thoughts uncertain. A glance can suggest a possibility without proving it.
evidence: it would have been hard to discover

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy — brief excerpt: Higgins says thank you
days.challenge: Infer a speaker’s hesitation without assuming only one possible feeling.
days.focus: A person with little social power meets a child with unexpected influence.
days.context: After the church service, Higgins waits to thank the boy whose letter helped him. His family had faced illness and financial trouble. Try the short scene independently, with an adult available for “landlord” and “lordship”; then reread the pauses in the conversation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII.; contiguous excerpt, 8 source blocks; opens “As they came out of the church, many of those who had …”; closes “… deal to thank your lordship for," he said; "a great deal. I——"”.

blocks.text: As they came out of the church, many of those who had attended the service stood waiting to see them pass. As they neared the gate, a man who stood with his hat in his hand made a step forward and then hesitated. He was a middle-aged farmer, with a careworn face.
"Well, Higgins," said the Earl.
Fauntleroy turned quickly to look at him.
"Oh!" he exclaimed; "is it Mr. Higgins?"
"Yes," answered the Earl dryly; "and I suppose he came to take a look at his new landlord."

"Yes, my lord," said the man, his sunburned face reddening. "Mr. Newick told me his young lordship was kind enough to speak for me, and I thought I'd like to say a word of thanks, if I might be allowed."

Perhaps he felt some wonder when he saw what a little fellow it was who had innocently done so much for him, and who stood there looking up just as one of his own less fortunate children might have done—apparently not realizing his own importance in the least.
"I've a great deal to thank your lordship for," he said; "a great deal. I——"

questions.prompt: What action shows that Higgins is unsure about approaching?
facilitatorNotes: He steps forward and then hesitates, holding his hat. Respect, nerves or uncertainty are supported possibilities.
evidence: made a step forward and then hesitated

questions.prompt: What has Higgins heard about Cedric’s part in helping him?
facilitatorNotes: Newick told him the boy spoke on his behalf. He is coming to thank the person he believes intervened.
evidence: his young lordship was kind enough to speak for me

questions.prompt: Why is the narrator’s comparison with Higgins’s own children meaningful?
facilitatorNotes: Cedric has the same small, childlike appearance despite much greater social power. The comparison highlights the gap between ordinary childhood and inherited status.
evidence: just as one of his own less fortunate children might have done

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy — excerpt: the Earl hears a surprising description
days.challenge: Notice dramatic irony: readers and adults know something the child does not.
days.focus: A child’s sincere praise places pressure on an adult’s public behaviour.
days.context: Higgins has thanked Cedric for helping his family. Cedric gives the credit to his grandfather, unaware that Higgins knows the Earl’s less generous reputation.
days.contentNote: A past outbreak of scarlet fever and the Earl’s neglect of his children are discussed without describing symptoms or injury. The text’s relief from worry is part of the story, not a claim that worry alone causes illness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII.; contiguous excerpt, 7 source blocks; opens “"Oh," said Fauntleroy; "I only wrote the letter. It was my grandfather …”; closes “… the corner into the high road, the Earl was still grimly smiling.”.

blocks.text: "Oh," said Fauntleroy; "I only wrote the letter. It was my grandfather who did it. But you know how he is about always being good to everybody. Is Mrs. Higgins well now?"
Higgins looked a trifle taken aback. He also was somewhat startled at hearing his noble landlord presented in the character of a benevolent being, full of engaging qualities.
"I—well, yes, your lordship," he stammered; "the missus is better since the trouble was took off her mind. It was worrying broke her down."
"I'm glad of that," said Fauntleroy. "My grandfather was very sorry about your children having the scarlet fever, and so was I. He has had children himself. I'm his son's little boy, you know."

Higgins was on the verge of being panic-stricken. He felt it would be the safer and more discreet plan not to look at the Earl, as it had been well known that his fatherly affection for his sons had been such that he had seen them about twice a year, and that when they had been ill, he had promptly departed for London, because he would not be bored with doctors and nurses. It was a little trying therefore to his lordship's nerves to be told, while he looked on, his eyes gleaming from under his shaggy eyebrows, that he felt an interest in scarlet fever.

"You see, Higgins," broke in the Earl with a fine grim smile; "you people have been mistaken in me. Lord Fauntleroy understands me. When you want reliable information on the subject of my character, apply to him. Get into the carriage, Fauntleroy."
And Fauntleroy jumped in, and the carriage rolled away down the green lane, and even when it turned the corner into the high road, the Earl was still grimly smiling.

questions.prompt: How does Cedric divide the credit for helping Higgins?
facilitatorNotes: He says he only wrote the letter and his grandfather acted. He does not claim all the credit because people are thanking him.
evidence: I only wrote the letter. It was my grandfather who did it.

questions.prompt: Why is Higgins startled by Cedric’s account of the Earl?
facilitatorNotes: He knows the Earl has not usually behaved as a caring father or generous landlord. The contrast makes the praise uncomfortable.
evidence: presented in the character of a benevolent being

questions.prompt: What makes the Earl’s suggestion to ask Cedric about his character ironic?
facilitatorNotes: Cedric is sincere but lacks the knowledge the others possess. The Earl can enjoy the flattering account while readers hear its mismatch with his past.
evidence: When you want reliable information on the subject of my character, apply to him.

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, chapter XIV excerpt: An invitation to come home
days.challenge: Infer changed feelings from a greeting, an invitation, and an apparently contradictory final sentence.
days.focus: A reunion matters more to the child than the restoration of his title.
days.context: Cedric Errol, called Lord Fauntleroy, is the Earl’s grandson. A claim that another boy should inherit has just proved false. The Earl has previously kept Cedric’s mother living separately from them; now he visits her house. Read the dialogue yourself first, then reread the last exchange together.
days.contentNote: Burnett’s story turns on inherited titles; much of its feeling comes from Cedric caring more about people than about rank.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 17 source blocks; opens “When the Earl left the room after the interview, he went at …”; closes “… we were not exactly aware of it. We hope you will come.””.

blocks.text: When the Earl left the room after the interview, he went at once to his carriage.
“To Court Lodge,” he said to Thomas.
“To Court Lodge,” said Thomas to the coachman as he mounted the box; “an’ you may depend on it, things is taking a uniggspected turn.”
When the carriage stopped at Court Lodge, Cedric was in the drawing-room with his mother.
The Earl came in without being announced. He looked an inch or so taller, and a great many years younger. His deep eyes flashed.
“Where,” he said, “is Lord Fauntleroy?”
Mrs. Errol came forward, a flush rising to her cheek.
“Is it Lord Fauntleroy?” she asked. “Is it, indeed!”
The Earl put out his hand and grasped hers.
“Yes,” he answered, “it is.”
Then he put his other hand on Cedric’s shoulder.
“Fauntleroy,” he said in his unceremonious, authoritative way, “ask your mother when she will come to us at the Castle.”
Fauntleroy flung his arms around his mother’s neck.
“To live with us!” he cried. “To live with us always!”

The Earl looked at Mrs. Errol, and Mrs. Errol looked at the Earl. His lordship was entirely in earnest. He had made up his mind to waste no time in arranging this matter. He had begun to think it would suit him to make friends with his heir’s mother.
“Are you quite sure you want me?” said Mrs. Errol, with her soft, pretty smile.
“Quite sure,” he said bluntly. “We have always wanted you, but we were not exactly aware of it. We hope you will come.”

questions.prompt: What news does the Earl communicate simply by asking for Lord Fauntleroy?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes Cedric as the rightful holder of the title again. Mrs. Errol’s surprised question confirms that the name itself carries important news.
evidence: “Is it Lord Fauntleroy?” she asked.

questions.prompt: Which part of the news makes Cedric throw his arms around his mother?
facilitatorNotes: The invitation means she can live with him at the Castle. His repeated always emphasizes reunion and permanence rather than possessions.
evidence: “To live with us always!”

questions.prompt: How can the Earl say they always wanted her while admitting they were not aware of it?
facilitatorNotes: He is newly recognizing the family connection he previously resisted. Readers may hear an indirect apology or an awkward admission of changed understanding; neither requires him to have consciously wanted her all along.
evidence: we were not exactly aware of it

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, chapter XV excerpt: Futures for the friends
days.challenge: Follow how the narrator gives several characters different futures before returning to the coming birthday.
days.focus: A resolution extends care beyond the central character.
days.context: The inheritance dispute is over. Ben and his son Tom return to California; Dick and Mr. Hobbs are Cedric’s old friends from New York. Mr. Havisham is the family lawyer. An adult can explain investment as providing money to establish a business, and tenants as people who rent homes or land.
days.contentNote: The Earl’s wealth allows him to offer opportunities; the passage describes this story’s circumstances, not a guarantee that effort or kindness always brings money.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 3 source blocks; opens “Ben took his boy and went back to his cattle ranch in …”; closes “… the Fourth, doesn’t it? For then we could keep them both together.””.

blocks.text: Ben took his boy and went back to his cattle ranch in California, and he returned under very comfortable circumstances. Just before his going, Mr. Havisham had an interview with him in which the lawyer told him that the Earl of Dorincourt wished to do something for the boy who might have turned out to be Lord Fauntleroy, and so he had decided that it would be a good plan to invest in a cattle ranch of his own, and put Ben in charge of it on terms which would make it pay him very well, and which would lay a foundation for his son’s future. And so when Ben went away, he went as the prospective master of a ranch which would be almost as good as his own, and might easily become his own in time, as indeed it did in the course of a few years; and Tom, the boy, grew up on it into a fine young man and was devotedly fond of his father; and they were so successful and happy that Ben used to say that Tom made up to him for all the troubles he had ever had.

But Dick and Mr. Hobbs—who had actually come over with the others to see that things were properly looked after—did not return for some time. It had been decided at the outset that the Earl would provide for Dick, and would see that he received a solid education; and Mr. Hobbs had decided that as he himself had left a reliable substitute in charge of his store, he could afford to wait to see the festivities, which were to celebrate Lord Fauntleroy’s eighth birthday. All the tenantry were invited, and there were to be feasting and dancing and games in the park, and bonfires and fireworks in the evening.
“Just like the Fourth of July!” said Lord Fauntleroy. “It seems a pity my birthday wasn’t on the Fourth, doesn’t it? For then we could keep them both together.”

questions.prompt: How do the Earl’s plans for Ben and Tom differ from his plan for Dick?
facilitatorNotes: Ben receives responsibility for a ranch that can support Tom’s future; Dick is to receive an education. The help responds to different situations rather than giving everyone the same thing.
evidence: he received a solid education

questions.prompt: What practical arrangement lets Mr. Hobbs remain for Cedric’s birthday?
facilitatorNotes: A reliable substitute is running his store, so he can stay without leaving the business unattended. This small detail makes the visit possible.
evidence: left a reliable substitute in charge of his store

questions.prompt: Why does Cedric connect the planned party with the Fourth of July?
facilitatorNotes: The feasting, games, bonfires, and fireworks remind him of the American celebration. His wish to combine them joins a familiar childhood memory to his new English life.
evidence: For then we could keep them both together.

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, chapter XV excerpt: A room full of ancestors
days.challenge: Use sound and the surrounding details to explain why one unfamiliar word creates a large misunderstanding.
days.focus: Grand surroundings become a comic scene through a visitor’s mistaken hearing.
days.context: Cedric shows Mr. Hobbs around the Castle. An ancestor is a family member from an earlier generation; progeny means descendants or children. Read the short dialogue yourself, then reread it aloud to hear the misunderstanding.
days.contentNote: The author represents Mr. Hobbs’s speech with dialect spellings and contrasts social backgrounds; unfamiliarity with a word does not make someone less worthy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 6 source blocks; opens “It must be confessed that at first the Earl and Mr. Hobbs …”; closes “… not lined entirely with the portraits of the progeny of his great-uncle.”.

blocks.text: It must be confessed that at first the Earl and Mr. Hobbs were not as intimate as it might have been hoped they would become, in the interests of the British aristocracy. The fact was that the Earl had known very few grocery-men, and Mr. Hobbs had not had many very close acquaintances who were earls; and so in their rare interviews conversation did not flourish. It must also be owned that Mr. Hobbs had been rather overwhelmed by the splendors Fauntleroy felt it his duty to show him.

The entrance gate and the stone lions and the avenue impressed Mr. Hobbs somewhat at the beginning, and when he saw the Castle, and the flower-gardens, and the hot-houses, and the terraces, and the peacocks, and the dungeon, and the armor, and the great staircase, and the stables, and the liveried servants, he really was quite bewildered. But it was the picture gallery which seemed to be the finishing stroke.
“Somethin’ in the manner of a museum?” he said to Fauntleroy, when he was led into the great, beautiful room.
“N—no—!” said Fauntleroy, rather doubtfully. “I don’t think it’s a museum. My grandfather says these are my ancestors.”
“Your aunt’s sisters!” ejaculated Mr. Hobbs. “All of ’em? Your great-uncle, he must have had a family! Did he raise ’em all?”

And he sank into a seat and looked around him with quite an agitated countenance, until with the greatest difficulty Lord Fauntleroy managed to explain that the walls were not lined entirely with the portraits of the progeny of his great-uncle.

questions.prompt: What suggests that Mr. Hobbs is overwhelmed before the conversation in the gallery begins?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator piles up an extensive list of grand sights and says he is bewildered. The gallery is the finishing stroke after many surprises.
evidence: he really was quite bewildered

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Hobbs hear instead of ancestors, and why does that make the number of portraits surprising?
facilitatorNotes: He hears aunt’s sisters and imagines they are all children of one great-uncle. That misunderstanding turns many generations into one enormous family.
evidence: Your aunt’s sisters!

questions.prompt: Why is Cedric’s answer about the museum hesitant rather than confident?
facilitatorNotes: The gallery resembles a museum to a visitor, but Cedric knows the pictures through his grandfather’s explanation of family history. His broken opening and I don’t think show uncertainty about the category.
evidence: “N—no—!” said Fauntleroy, rather doubtfully.

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, chapter XV excerpt: The stories behind the pictures
days.challenge: Compare the visitor’s repeated actions with his eventual admission, and distinguish fascination from proof of a political belief.
days.focus: Learning a story can change how someone looks at an unfamiliar place.
days.context: Mr. Hobbs has mistaken ancestors for aunt’s sisters. Cedric asks Mrs. Mellon, who knows the Castle and its history, to explain the portraits. Here republican principles means preferring government without inherited noble rulers; it is not a reference to a present-day political party.
days.contentNote: The narrator finds humor in Mr. Hobbs’s attraction to aristocratic luxury. Enjoying impressive surroundings does not prove that inherited social rank is fair.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 4 source blocks; opens “He found it necessary, in fact, to call in the assistance of …”; closes “… bein’ one of ’em myself!” he said—which was really a great concession.”.

blocks.text: He found it necessary, in fact, to call in the assistance of Mrs. Mellon, who knew all about the pictures, and could tell who painted them and when, and who added romantic stories of the lords and ladies who were the originals. When Mr. Hobbs once understood, and had heard some of these stories, he was very much fascinated and liked the picture gallery almost better than anything else; and he would often walk over from the village where he staid at the Dorincourt Arms, and would spend half an hour or so wandering about the gallery, staring at the painted ladies and gentlemen who also stared at him, and shaking his head nearly all the time.
“And they was all earls!” he would say, “er pretty nigh it! An’ he’s goin’ to be one of ’em, an’ own it all!”

Privately he was not nearly so much disgusted with earls and their mode of life as he had expected to be, and it is to be doubted whether his strictly republican principles were not shaken a little by a closer acquaintance with castles and ancestors and all the rest of it. At any rate, one day he uttered a very remarkable and unexpected sentiment:
“I wouldn’t have minded bein’ one of ’em myself!” he said—which was really a great concession.

questions.prompt: What does Mrs. Mellon add that makes the portraits more interesting to Mr. Hobbs?
facilitatorNotes: She identifies the artists and dates and tells stories about the people pictured. The faces acquire histories rather than remaining an unexplained collection.
evidence: romantic stories of the lords and ladies

questions.prompt: How can readers tell his interest lasts beyond that first explanation?
facilitatorNotes: He repeatedly walks from the village and spends time looking at the gallery. His return visits supply stronger evidence than a single polite compliment would.
evidence: he would often walk over from the village

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator call his last remark a great concession?
facilitatorNotes: He expected to dislike earls and their way of life, but admits that he would not mind sharing it. This reveals attraction and a softened attitude, rather than proving every earlier principle wrong.
evidence: I wouldn’t have minded bein’ one of ’em myself!

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, chapter XV excerpt: Old friends at the birthday
days.challenge: Track several social groups in a crowded scene and connect a small act of welcome to Cedric’s happiness.
days.focus: A celebration joins old friendships with a changed family life.
days.context: The Earl’s tenants, neighbors, and guests gather for Cedric’s eighth birthday. Miss Herbert is a friend he admires, and he has promised that his old American friends will meet her. Read the long opening together, then let the child choose a paragraph to reread.
days.contentNote: The story emphasizes noble titles, appearance, and a woman’s beauty in ways typical of its period; kindness can be considered separately from those judgments.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 7 source blocks; opens “What a grand day it was when little Lord Fauntleroy’s birthday arrived, …”; closes “The whole world seemed beautiful to him.”.

blocks.text: What a grand day it was when little Lord Fauntleroy’s birthday arrived, and how his young lordship enjoyed it! How beautiful the park looked, filled with the thronging people dressed in their gayest and best, and with the flags flying from the tents and the top of the Castle! Nobody had staid away who could possibly come, because everybody was really glad that little Lord Fauntleroy was to be little Lord Fauntleroy still, and some day was to be the master of everything. Every one wanted to have a look at him, and at his pretty, kind mother, who had made so many friends. And positively every one liked the Earl rather better, and felt more amiably toward him because the little boy loved and trusted him so, and because, also, he had now made friends with and behaved respectfully to his heir’s mother. It was said that he was even beginning to be fond of her, too, and that between his young lordship and his young lordship’s mother, the Earl might be changed in time into quite a well-behaved old nobleman, and everybody might be happier and better off.

What scores and scores of people there were under the trees, and in the tents, and on the lawns! Farmers and farmers’ wives in their Sunday suits and bonnets and shawls; girls and their sweethearts; children frolicking and chasing about; and old dames in red cloaks gossiping together. At the Castle, there were ladies and gentlemen who had come to see the fun, and to congratulate the Earl, and to meet Mrs. Errol. Lady Lorredaile and Sir Harry were there, and Sir Thomas Asshe and his daughters, and Mr. Havisham, of course, and then beautiful Miss Vivian Herbert, with the loveliest white gown and lace parasol, and a circle of gentlemen to take care of her—though she evidently liked Fauntleroy better than all of them put together. And when he saw her and ran to her and put his arm around her neck, she put her arms around him, too, and kissed him as warmly as if he had been her own favorite little brother, and she said:
“Dear little Lord Fauntleroy! dear little boy! I am so glad! I am so glad!”

And afterward she walked about the grounds with him, and let him show her everything. And when he took her to where Mr. Hobbs and Dick were, and said to her, “This is my old, old friend Mr. Hobbs, Miss Herbert, and this is my other old friend Dick. I told them how pretty you were, and I told them they should see you if you came to my birthday,”—she shook hands with them both, and stood and talked to them in her prettiest way, asking them about America and their voyage and their life since they had been in England; while Fauntleroy stood by, looking up at her with adoring eyes, and his cheeks quite flushed with delight because he saw that Mr. Hobbs and Dick liked her so much.
“Well,” said Dick solemnly, afterward, “she’s the daisiest gal I ever saw! She’s—well, she’s just a daisy, that’s what she is, ’n no mistake!”

Everybody looked after her as she passed, and every one looked after little Lord Fauntleroy. And the sun shone and the flags fluttered and the games were played and the dances danced, and as the gayeties went on and the joyous afternoon passed, his little lordship was simply radiantly happy.
The whole world seemed beautiful to him.

questions.prompt: Why do the guests view the Earl more warmly than before?
facilitatorNotes: They see Cedric’s love and trust and the Earl’s new respect for Cedric’s mother. The improved relationships change how people judge him.
evidence: behaved respectfully to his heir’s mother

questions.prompt: How does Miss Herbert make Mr. Hobbs and Dick feel included?
facilitatorNotes: She shakes their hands and asks about their home, voyage, and experience in England. Her questions show interest in their lives rather than merely acknowledging an introduction.
evidence: asking them about America and their voyage

questions.prompt: What effect does the repeated and have in the paragraph about sunshine, flags, games, and dances?
facilitatorNotes: It carries one happy activity into the next, creating an accumulating sense of movement and abundance. Invite the child to read the sentence aloud and notice its rhythm.
evidence: And the sun shone and the flags fluttered

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, chapter XV excerpt: A beginning of kindness
days.challenge: Distinguish a narrator’s qualified account of gradual change from a claim that a person has suddenly become perfect.
days.focus: Affection and practiced kindness matter more than inherited grandeur.
days.context: During Cedric’s birthday, the narrator turns from the child to his grandfather. The Earl has been wealthy for a long time but has only recently begun caring openly for Cedric and his mother. Read the reflective sentences together, then identify what has and has not changed.
days.contentNote: The narrator uses class and gender judgments such as well-bred and manly. The passage’s kindness can be discussed without treating wealth, rank, or masculinity as measures of worth.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 2 source blocks; opens “There was some one else who was happy, too,—an old man, who, …”; closes “… simple and loving. To be so is like being born a king.”.

blocks.text: There was some one else who was happy, too,—an old man, who, though he had been rich and noble all his life, had not often been very honestly happy. Perhaps, indeed, I shall tell you that I think it was because he was rather better than he had been that he was rather happier. He had not, indeed, suddenly become as good as Fauntleroy thought him; but, at least, he had begun to love something, and he had several times found a sort of pleasure in doing the kind things which the innocent, kind little heart of a child had suggested,—and that was a beginning. And every day he had been more pleased with his son’s wife. It was true, as the people said, that he was beginning to like her too. He liked to hear her sweet voice and to see her sweet face; and as he sat in his armchair, he used to watch her and listen as she talked to her boy; and he heard loving, gentle words which were new to him, and he began to see why the little fellow who had lived in a New York side street and known grocery-men and made friends with boot-blacks, was still so well-bred and manly a little fellow that he made no one ashamed of him, even when fortune changed him into the heir to an English earldom, living in an English castle.

It was really a very simple thing, after all,—it was only that he had lived near a kind and gentle heart, and had been taught to think kind thoughts always and to care for others. It is a very little thing, perhaps, but it is the best thing of all. He knew nothing of earls and castles; he was quite ignorant of all grand and splendid things; but he was always lovable because he was simple and loving. To be so is like being born a king.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator mention that the Earl was rich long before he was happy?
facilitatorNotes: The contrast suggests that possessions and rank did not themselves give him the happiness he now finds in affection and kind actions. Keep the answer tied to this character rather than making a rule about every wealthy person.
evidence: had not often been very honestly happy

questions.prompt: Which words keep the Earl’s improvement from sounding complete?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says he has not suddenly become as good as Cedric imagines and calls his progress a beginning. The qualification makes room for continued growth.
evidence: and that was a beginning

questions.prompt: What does the comparison to being born a king mean at the end?
facilitatorNotes: It gives the dignity usually attached to rank to a loving character instead. Cedric’s value comes from how he treats people, even when he knows nothing of castles.
evidence: he was always lovable because he was simple and loving

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, chapter XV excerpt: Cedric’s thank-you speech
days.challenge: Use the sound of a speech and the speaker’s gestures to infer nervousness, gratitude, and trust.
days.focus: A child’s public gratitude reveals both confidence and vulnerability.
days.context: At the birthday feast, the tenants raise a toast, a spoken wish for someone’s well-being. Collation means a light meal or refreshments. Cedric is asked to thank them. Read the speech yourself first; an adult can help with the longer opening paragraph.
days.contentNote: Guests drink ceremonial toasts; the passage does not specify the drink. Historical class distinctions shape the gathering.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 11 source blocks; opens “As the old Earl of Dorincourt looked at him that day, moving …”; closes “… Earl’s and stood close to him, smiling and leaning against his side.”.

blocks.text: As the old Earl of Dorincourt looked at him that day, moving about the park among the people, talking to those he knew and making his ready little bow when any one greeted him, entertaining his friends Dick and Mr. Hobbs, or standing near his mother or Miss Herbert listening to their conversation, the old nobleman was very well satisfied with him. And he had never been better satisfied than he was when they went down to the biggest tent, where the more important tenants of the Dorincourt estate were sitting down to the grand collation of the day.

They were drinking toasts; and, after they had drunk the health of the Earl, with much more enthusiasm than his name had ever been greeted with before, they proposed the health of “Little Lord Fauntleroy.” And if there had ever been any doubt at all as to whether his lordship was popular or not, it would have been settled that instant. Such a clamor of voices, and such a rattle of glasses and applause! They had begun to like him so much, those warm-hearted people, that they forgot to feel any restraint before the ladies and gentlemen from the castle, who had come to see them. They made quite a decent uproar, and one or two motherly women looked tenderly at the little fellow where he stood, with his mother on one side and the Earl on the other, and grew quite moist about the eyes, and said to one another:
“God bless him, the pretty little dear!”
Little Lord Fauntleroy was delighted. He stood and smiled, and made bows, and flushed rosy red with pleasure up to the roots of his bright hair.
“Is it because they like me, Dearest?” he said to his mother. “Is it, Dearest? I’m so glad!”
And then the Earl put his hand on the child’s shoulder and said to him:
“Fauntleroy, say to them that you thank them for their kindness.”
Fauntleroy gave a glance up at him and then at his mother.

“Must I!” he asked just a trifle shyly, and she smiled, and so did Miss Herbert, and they both nodded. And so he made a little step forward, and everybody looked at him—such a beautiful, innocent little fellow he was, too, with his brave trustful face!—and he spoke as loudly as he could, his childish voice ringing out quite clear and strong.

“I’m ever so much obliged to you!” he said, “and—I hope you’ll enjoy my birthday—because I’ve enjoyed it so much—and—I’m very glad I’m going to be an earl—I didn’t think at first I should like it, but now I do—and I love this place so, and I think it is beautiful—and—and—and when I am an earl, I am going to try to be as good as my grandfather.”
And amid the shouts and clamor of applause, he stepped back with a little sigh of relief, and put his hand into the Earl’s and stood close to him, smiling and leaning against his side.

questions.prompt: What evidence shows the guests feel more than polite approval of Cedric?
facilitatorNotes: Their loud applause, clamor, and emotional reactions overwhelm their usual restraint around the Castle guests. The narrator shows feeling through noise and tears.
evidence: Such a clamor of voices, and such a rattle of glasses and applause!

questions.prompt: How do the repeated ands and the final sigh help you imagine Cedric delivering the speech?
facilitatorNotes: He searches for what to say while speaking eagerly, then relaxes when it is over. Read the pauses naturally rather than treating the repetitions as mistakes to erase.
evidence: a little sigh of relief

questions.prompt: Why does Cedric’s wish to be as good as his grandfather mean more after the earlier passage about the Earl?
facilitatorNotes: Cedric trusts an ideal version of the Earl, while readers know the man is still changing. His admiration may encourage the grandfather to live up to that trust; this is an interpretation, not a guaranteed result.
evidence: I am going to try to be as good as my grandfather

days.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy, final excerpt: Mr. Hobbs stays nearby
days.challenge: Connect a closing joke with an earlier scene while separating the character’s stated reason from the narrator’s additional explanation.
days.focus: An ending preserves a friendship while showing how a visitor has changed.
days.context: After the birthday speech, the narrator adds a glimpse of later years. Dick has completed his education, and Mr. Hobbs has made a new home. Reread the final spoken lines after recalling his earlier misunderstanding of ancestors.
days.contentNote: Mr. Hobbs’s comments about America and England are his personal opinions in the story, not descriptions that apply to everyone in either country.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, October 1886 serial; contiguous excerpt, 2 source blocks; opens “And that would be the very end of my story; but I …”; closes “… there’s faults in it. There’s not an auntsister among ’em—nor a earl!””.

blocks.text: And that would be the very end of my story; but I must add one curious piece of information, which is that Mr. Hobbs became so fascinated with high life and was so reluctant to leave his young friend that he actually sold his corner store in New York, and settled in the English village of Erlesboro, where he opened a shop which was patronized by the Castle and consequently was a great success. And though he and the Earl never became very intimate, if you will believe me, that man Hobbs became in time more aristocratic than his lordship himself, and he read the Court news every morning, and followed all the doings of the House of Lords! And about ten years after, when Dick, who had finished his education and was going to visit his brother in California, asked the good grocer if he did not wish to return to America, he shook his head seriously.

“Not to live there,” he said. “Not to live there; I want to be near him, an’ sort o’ look after him. It’s a good enough country for them that’s young an’ stirrin’—but there’s faults in it. There’s not an auntsister among ’em—nor a earl!”

questions.prompt: What two attractions does the narrator give for Mr. Hobbs’s decision to settle in England?
facilitatorNotes: He likes high society and is reluctant to leave Cedric. The account allows affection and fascination with status to coexist.
evidence: so fascinated with high life and was so reluctant to leave his young friend

questions.prompt: Why does the success of his new shop make sense within the story?
facilitatorNotes: The Castle patronizes it, supplying customers and business support. His friendship and location connect to the practical outcome.
evidence: patronized by the Castle and consequently was a great success

questions.prompt: How does the last use of auntsister link the ending to the portrait-gallery scene?
facilitatorNotes: It recalls his mishearing of ancestors, though he now values the aristocratic history he once found confusing. The repeated joke leaves him changed but still recognizably himself.
evidence: There’s not an auntsister among ’em—nor a earl!
